Official Report
On the orders of the day:

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called I should like to draw your attention to an error in yesterday's Hansard. When the orders of the day were called yesterday the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) rose in his place and read a carefully prepared statement to the house, at the conclusion of which he stated that one page had been omitted from his notes. He then retired from the chamber and the house proceeded with ordinary routine business. Returning to the chamber in about three-quarters of an hour the Prime Minister read his entire statement, including the page which had been omitted. I find on looking up Hansard this morning that the Prime Minister's original statement, together with certain remarks that were made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Manion) have been omitted from Hansard. My question is:	On what authority is this being
done?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say first to my hon. friend that I had nothing whatever to do with the matter myself. The arrangement of Hansard is in the hands of the Hansard staff. Where on previous occasions there have been obvious omissions or transpositions of some kind, in the arrangement of Hansard those omissions or transpositions are usually dealt with as the editor of a paper would deal with any matter of the kind in presenting it in its final form. I inquired last night as to what Hansard proposed to do, whether it was proposed to insert verbatim et literatim the little interjections with regard to a page being missed out of my statement and the whole repeated as reread. I was informed that Hansard proposed to have the matter printed as if the page had not been omitted, and simply give the full account as was originally intended and as subsequently read. I understood that Hansard-I may be wrong-before taking that step had intended to speak to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) to see if he would have any objection, but the leader of the opposition not being here in the evening, I am informed the matter was then referred to the chief whip of the Conservative party. That is what I am informed. The chief whip, I was told, said he thought it would be quite right to have Hansard printed without indicating the brief exchange concerning the omission of a page that had taken place. I believe that was the courtesy which was extended by hon. gentlemen opposite-I may be wrong. But certainly
I should think in any circumstances it was quite a proper thing for Hansard to have done. If I had altered any sentence or remark in the second reading of the statement as read on the first occasion or had in any way sought to deceive the house about what was purely an omission occasioned by a failure on the part of a stenographer to copy one of the concluding pages, I think there would have been something to the point which my hon. friend has raised. But for the purpose of the intelligent reading of Hansard as a matter of record I think it was much better to have repetition avoided and the complete statement put in the form in which it was.
I may say to my hon. friend that when I came back into the house with the complete statement the hon. leader of the opposition indicated to me across the floor of the house that it might be best to read it from the beginning in its entirety so that all members would have the complete context, and I did that. I thought at the time my hon. friend was seeking to assure me that that would be the best way of proceeding, if I was to have the statement in its entirety' as it appeared'. I am giving my hon. friend the situation as I understand it. If there has been any fault in the matter, I hope it will be put on my shoulders as leader of the house. If Hansard were to come to me and ask me what I thought was correct in the matter of reporting the proceedings of the house in a case of that kind, I would say it was much better to have Hansard state the situation as hon. members would wish to see it stated, rather than in any way unnecessarily to burden Hansard with something that did not affect the proceedings.

I had no idea that the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) and the Conservative whip (Mr. Casselman) had agreed to this. I simply saw in Hansard that it had been omitted. During this session there have been several omissions from Hansard, and I wish to protest against omissions being made from Hansard by any person, or Hansard having authority to make these changes.
If, as the hon. member suggests, there were omissions before the occurrence of yesterday, he should have drawn the attention of the house to them, and they would have been dealt with accordingly.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) I think it is incumbent upon me to say something. I understand the right hon. gentleman to say that I did concur in

the deletion from Hansard. It is quite true that Mr. Young, the editor of debates, communicated with me last night and asked me if I would acquiesce in such a change. I told him that at that time I would not acquiesce, that I had no authority to assume to myself any responsibilities that are covered by the rules of the house. In order that there should be no misunderstanding, I took the matter up with the editor of debates before the opening of the house to-day, believing that he might have misunderstood me. In conversation with me he stated positively that I did not acquiesce in any change.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I apologize then to my hon. friend and to the entire house. I can only say that I made inquiry last night of my secretary who reported the circumstances to me exactly as I have given them to the house. I have not had a word with him since, and I let the matter drop at that stage. As a matter of fact what I suggested to my secretary was that he should see the Speaker and ask him about it. His reply to me was that the whip of the Conservative party. had already indicated he thought that that would be a perfectly correct procedure. If the house thinks that Hansard ought to be reprinted with the correction to which my hon. friend has drawn attention, I :am perfectly agreeable. I must confess that I cannot see where there has been any attempt to invade any privilege either of the house or of its individual members.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did nod across to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) yesterday and I concurred with him in the suggestion that he read the whole statement from the beginning in view of the fact that he had read part of it and then stated he had forgotten a page which he brought in later. I wanted to hear the whole statement read continuously. I had no intention of bringing up this matter, but since it has been brought up I do not think that this is a question of the details concerned. I admit perhaps that there has been no change made in the ideas or substance of the statement in any shape or form; there is no suggestion of that. The Prime Minister says that he did not have it done, and he mentions that the editor of Hansard or someone on his behalf endeavoured to get in touch with me. My secretary told me this morning that that is correct. I went home from this house yesterday afternoon with quite a cold, and I decided that the telephone should not bother me all evening; I gave instructions that it should not be answered I think it rang at
(Mr. Casselman.]
least a dozen times, which is probably eleven times too many. I would not answer it and I refused to let anybody else in the house answer it. I wanted to go to bed to rest.
The point I should like to make is Ibis. There is no question of a change in the context because I understand there was none except that the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) does mention that I said a few words. If I recall, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) said a few words. We both did, and they were both cut out. Not that my remarks were probably of any importance anyway, but I do deny to the editor of Hansard or to anybody else the right to remove anything said by me without my consent. I was twitted across the floor of the house the other night for having changed a word in Hansard. Incidentally I have searched that since, and my secretary, who is really to blame if anybody was, as he checks over Hansard, as to my remarks, and we find there was no change. However, to-day two or three pages have been cut out of Hansard by the editor of Hansard apparently without the consent of the Speaker and of both sides of the house. That seems to me to be a most extraordinary proceeding. Therefore, I wish to say this:	I do not think the editor of
Hansard has any right at any time to cut out two or three pages of Hansard without any excuse whatsoever unless he gets the consent probably of the leaders of all parties and the Speaker as well. I think it is too serious a matter to have the editor of Hansard have the power in his hands to do any such thing.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) asked me on March 13 when I expected to receive the so-called Rowell commission report. I replied that the last time I had had word with the chairman of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations was at the beginning of the year so that I might advise parliament when parliament met, and that I was then informed that the commission hoped to have their report ready about Easter. I added that I was sorry I was unable to say whether they were still of that opinion. The following day, that is, on March 14, I wrote the chairman of the commission and drew his attention to the question of the leader of the opposition, and I have received from him the following reply:
Royal commission on dominion-provincial relations
Ottawa, March 15, 1939. The Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, M.P.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa.
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,
I have your letter of March 14 inquiring when the commission's report will be ready. -
When we last met I mentioned that the commission hoped to have the report completed about Easter. Additional work and time, however, have been necessary on the public finance statistics and other basic studies, and it does not now appear possible that the report will be finished before July. We are making every effort to expedite the work, and if an earlier date of completion can be achieved, we shall be able to transmit the report to you somewhat sooner.
I am,
Dear Mr. Prime Minister,
Sincerely yours,
Jos. Sirois, Chairman.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I answer a question put yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). He asked:
In view of the international situation and reported suggestion for a conference of certain democratic powers, will the government consider the advisability of proposing a meeting of the League of Nations assembly with a view to formulating a joint policy for peace and with a view to seeking cooperation with the United States for such a policy?
The answer I would make to that question is as follows. In view of the fact that consultations have already been initiated by the countries immediately concerned, under the procedure they have considered appropriate for the stage that developments have reached, it is not considered advisable that the Canadian government put forward the suggested proposal.

speechtext:
Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker; although I do not wish to delay the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning), there is a matter which, with your permission, I should like to bring before the house for three or four minutes, and this is the only day this week on which it can be mentioned. I ask the government to clarify the statement which was made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) yesterday on foreign affairs and Canada's position. I agree with a great deal of what he said, and also with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) so well said. We should also, I say, have in this country a maximum of unity on these matters of national security and defence, and a minimum of criticism, because, as Adam Smith said, and do not forget that, security is better than opulence. At the same time I wish to point out that, although this is the forty-eighth day of the session, no action has been taken, the house does not know and the country cannot read between the lines and find out what is Canada's policy on this great question of life and death which confronts civilization to-day. Where is Canada, and what is she doing? It seems to me that Canada's policy is that "the pen is mightier than the sword"; but that is not so with Hitler and the other dictators. This land is much coveted by them because of its great natural resources and raw materials. I think the time has come when all the facts should be told and the country should be taken into the confidence of the government. I do not think we could do better than to follow the precedent in respect to publicity of facts set in England by Mr. Chamberlain, when, in his recent speech at the last dinner of the parliamentary press gallery in London, he said:
If the people are not allowed to know the facts; if they are only allowed to know what their rulers choose them to know, then that people are in danger of being led to embark upon a course which may presently lead them into disaster.
Speaking later in the House of Commons, he defined the country's commitments, gave the exact details and answered dozens of questions. I have examined day by day the London newspapers, particularly the Times,
2096	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
and I find that there was a very elaborate debate in the House of Commons the other day on this matter; almost every day the question is up there. One question which was then asked was, "Where is Canada?" Well, as I have said, we are at the forty-eighth day of the session, and parliament and the country are entitled to know, and we do not know as yet, where we are with regard to our security or defence on land, on the sea, or in the air. We have practically no defences except those supplied by the mother country as was the case in 1812. I believe that my honoured leader, who served so ably and faithfully in the war, gave a very fair statement as far as it goes, and I agree with him that we must not introduce politics into this matter or try to keep the country in the dark. Our silence is playing of politics. How is it that by leave of the radio commission this subject of defence of the realm and foreign affairs can be debated every Sunday and every day almost on the radio, yet this house is denied the right of knowing the facts which concern the security of Canada at this time? We do not know where we are. Italy and Japan our old allies have been driven since 1922 into the arms of Germany and very foolishly so; to-day Britain is "going it alone" with France. We should certainly know something more about what is going on.
I do not wish to embarrass the Prime Minister. Far from it; I should like to support him; and I believe the country, irrespective of class or creed or politics or anything else, will support him if he will do something. We do not know whether in Canada we are secure or not. Are we to wait until the enemy sails up the St. Lawrence? We know they can be here in a few hours if they come west instead of east, and they can by an air attack destroy every public utility in Montreal, Ottawa, Quebec, and Toronto in a few hours. The maritimes and Quebec will be the first to suffer. We know what a lack of defence policy and silence led to in 1914. The late Lord Roberts went up and down Great Britain and came to this country and told the people of the grave danger ahead, but his speeches were called pernicious and dangerous, even up to three days before the outbreak of war, because he predicted it and he had not a single statesman except Lord Milner with him. Are we going to repeat that in 1939 by our silence and lack of preparation before it is too late.
I am not going to take up any more time, because I should like to see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) get on with his work, 
but I believe that the time has come when we should have some action and an announcement from the government, or a day set aside soon so that the matter may be discussed.

of malleable, non-malleable and steel castings is concerned. Anyone who has had the privilege of going through the plants in the Pittsburgh area will realize this. Anyone who has high hopes of the city of Hamilton becoming the Pittsburgh of Canada will feel badly about this particular situation. I should like to make this observation. The entire concession in export schedules does not balance what has happened in concessions given in iron and steel imports alone.
Is the hon. member taking account of the free items?

The concessions granted by the United States by this trade treaty in connection with iron and steel products which might flow from Canada to the United States amount to only $13,696 on items over $25,000. That is the actual dollar value of the concessions they have given us in the iron and steel group. All the concessions granted in connection with goods entering the United States have a difference in the dollar value payable of $2,411,742. The concessions given by Canada in connection with iron and steel alone have a dollar value of $2,727,978 less duty to pay, apart entirely from the excise tax. I ask hon. members to carry this picture in their minds along with the picture given in the report on employment conditions in Canadian industry. We must remember that ever since 1927, 1928, 1929 and 1930 our friends in the United States have found themselves over-industrialized, especially in the iron and steel industry. It must be patent on the face of it that any action taken that will bring more of such products into this country will automatically-I do not like to use the word "paralyze"-still further handicap those of our citizens who are employed in the iron and steel industry. It is difficult for moulders of castings, such as are covered by item 390, when they reach the age of forty or fifty, to readjust themselves and enter some agricultural pursuit. They have probably started in as apprentices in the foundry at the age of fourteen or fifteen, and it is very hard for them to find themselves out of employment in middle life. They are a type of citizen who have their modest homes established near the centres of industry and probably pretty well paid for, and it is difficult for them to pick up and go into some other vocation or pursuit.
So I say that with this information in hand there should be more correlation between the activities in connection with this treaty and those of the Minister of Labour, who is charged with the responsibility of trying to find work for these 45,000 people. He should

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
have made strong representations that the people engaged in the iron and steel industry-should not be further handicapped by throwing open our markets by these tariff reductions -small reductions, I will admit, but nevertheless reductions which affect the very labour group which is suffering the most. I say that you want a strong Minister of Labour to administer that department, and I mean every word I say. The men in the industry affected by item 390 would gladly come to Ottawa and sit around a table with the Minister of Labour and with representatives of the Minister of Finance with a view to finding ways and means of expanding work in that particular industry so as to take up the slack.
I do not want to belabour the Minister of Finance; I do not want to worry him in any way whatsoever, and I hope he will not get up to reply to me. I do not feel that he should be charged with the responsibility of putting this treaty through the house in his present state of health. In fact, I stayed away from this treaty for a day or two to restrain myself, just because of the high regard I have for the Minister of Finance. But at the same time I have a duty to discharge, and when I say that the reduction made in items like 390, which is a representative item, will further restrict the possibility of the expansion of employment in the very group that is suffering the most, I say it most sincerely and with knowledge of what I am talking about.
I reiterate what I said in my opening remarks, that this committee is not supplied with the information necessary to enable it to deal intelligently with the items that we are asked to consider. Following the collapse of 1930, we had got back by 1935 some real activity in this line of business, but the action now taken in connection with this particular group of items is just enough to cripple a growing industry in such centres as Hamilton, Belleville and Toronto, and in the outskirts of Vancouver. Anyone in business knows that it takes so very little to switch an order for castings from one firm to another. They have codes and they try to adhere to fixed prices, as is done in other sections of the iron and steel group; although I must say at once to the credit of the Steel Company of Canada and our steel industry generally that they have kept their level of prices in Hamilton, for instance, lower than the level which obtains in Buffalo. They have not, in other words, taken full advantage of the tariff protection they have, with the net result that the minister could put his hand on any one of those seven hundred odd files which he was speaking of
with reference to this particular commodity and no doubt find a reference there from some of the larger steel industries to the effect that this trade treaty is not doing them very much harm because they played fair with the Canadian people and kept their price lower than the price which obtains in Buffalo. But now that you have narrowed that spread, you have got them closer to the Buffalo price, and so far as iron and steel products in the big sheets, rolls and bars are concerned, the industry is going to find it more difficult sledding. When you get down to castings such as are covered by item 390, you get down to the smaller industries, foundries and the like, all of which will find the orders they have been accustomed to receiving being bid on by other concerns, and the price cut finer. The net result will be that instead of an expansion of employment in this group where conditions are very serious we are likely to find a retraction of employment.
I will close this phase of my remarks by saying again that the schedules which have been most seriously disturbed are the very ones which affect the group in which we have the most serious situation in Canada as regards unemployment.
The other observation I shall make is this. It is far better, Mr. Chairman, to have a Canadian citizen working in the foundries of Canada or in the iron and steel industry of this country than for hon. members to sit around this house and discuss ways .and means of providing unemployment relief for those unfortunate Canadians who find themselves out of work.

I have gone with some care into iron and steel because it is an old friend of mine. I had to put through in 1930 the revision of the iron and steel schedule; and, while my friends behind me will not take it as much of a compliment, the succeeding government made less changes in that schedule than they did in any other. The reason was, I think, that there is such an inter-relationship from the primary products to the highly finished consumer's article in the iron and steel schedule that it is rather difficult to start anywhere without whatever action you take having an effect all up and down the line. In other words, unless you are prepared to revise the whole schedule with very great care, the iron and steel schedule is a difficult one to touch at merely one or two places.
That is about all I can say. It is true, as my hon. friend has stated, that the iron and steel industry has not indicated to me that they regard themselves as seriously affected by the new treaty. That is undoubtedly due, in part at least, to the fact that the Canadian iron and steel industry have not, generally speaking, taken advantage in their price structure of the tariff protection they have enjoyed. It is rather hard to make a generalization of that kind exactly accurate. It might not apply and in fact does not apply on some items, but I think it is generally true; and it is for that reason, possibly, that they do not regard themselves as seriously affected.

With regard to the question whether they consider themselves seriously affected, the minister will agree with me that as regards the major industry that is quite true. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am advised that the patent difficulty does not arise in connection with this class of electrical equipment. That is, there is a sufficient variety available to prevent any possibility of abuse in that direction. My hon. friend of course has reference particularly to radios and radio tubes. I should like to support the view expressed by the hon. member for Kootenay West. It is a principle which I think we in this country have to face. I had the matter up four years ago. In 1935 there was quite a discussion on it. At that time I think there were some amendments to the act. The matter has arisen on several occasions since. Unfortunately, when one mentions this subject, the tendency is for certain of our larger institutions, with which as institutions I have no quarrel, rather to take the attitude that you are attacking them. That is not the point at all. The real point is that there seems to be a confusion of the rights of the owner of a patent and the right of an individual to import.
I will illustrate the matter in this way. An article is patented; it is registered under the patent acts of the United States, Canada and other countries, under the general international arrangement. The royalty to the maker of the patented article is paid wherever the article is made. No one disputes that. I do not, and I do not think anyone does. But my point is that once the royalty is properly paid, whether in Canada, in Belgium, in Great Britain or in the United States, that is the sole right that the owner of the patent should be permitted to claim. In practice, however, this is what occurs. Usually the original inventor sells to some corporation, but we will stick to the simple illustration, taking the original inventor. He may sell his right to A in the United States, B in Canada and C in Great Britain. He sells the right to the royalty plus the right to manufacture. Then A, B and C argue that, having bought the right for the respective countries in which they operate, no one else has the right to sell the article in that market, even though he buys it in a market where the royalty has already been paid. That is an absolutely wrong principle, because obviously it means that one can impose a tariff, which might be 100 per cent or 500 per cent-that is, what is in effect a tariff-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Far more than a tariff.
It is not a tariff but the equivalent of a tariff. The article may be free, and-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The price differential may be 100 per cent.

Yes. As a matter of fact,
I illustrated it on a previous occasion with electric light bulbs, and as the hon. member for Kootenay West says, the same thing applies to a great many other articles.
One reason why nothing much is heard about the matter is that a great many of these articles are manufactured by concerns in the United States who establish agencies, in Canada, and they control the outlet in Canada, so that the point does not arise. But the purchaser is paying the shot, nevertheless.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would my hon. friend be good enough to develop the international patent agreement side of the question?

I must confess I am not quite competent to do that, because it is a matter for a legal mind rather than mine, but I will say this. The claim is made that where, in Canada for instance, a man secures the right to make and sell an article, that right to sell is inherent in the patent. My argument is that it is not. I believe there was a case before the exchequer court of Canada, and although I am not quite certain of this statement, I believe that court handed down a decision that the right was inherent in the patent by virtue of the statute as it stands.
My argument in 1935 was that we should so amend the patent law that while we absolutely preserved the protection to the inventor, we should not allow the right of control of sale to be attached to the patent, provided that the article that is imported has paid the royalty in the country from which it is imported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What bearing has the international agreement on that question? I am not familiar with it myself.

I have not looked the matter up. It is a complicated question and it is a little difficult for me to explain it from memory. Speaking subject to correction by some of the lawyers present, I understand that the international agreement does not interfere with the right of any country to make its own patent laws. There is nothing to prevent the parliament of Canada from amending, in any way it likes, its statutes controlling patents, provided that we do observe the registration of the invention under our law, just as any other country observes the registration of inventions at home under

their own laws. I am advised that there is nothing to prevent Canada or the United States or Germany or any other country from passing its own statutes controlling patents, in so far as the points I have mentioned are concerned, where sale and royalty are involved. For instance, we in our patent law declare that after a given number of years, if the invention is not used, the commissioner of patents may declare the patent open. That is a power which we reserve to ourselves. We fix a certain number of years and some other country may have a different period. I submit that there is nothing inherent in an invention that prevents Canada from passing its own statutory controlling law, although, as I say, I speak subject to correction.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My question was whether there was anything in the international agreement?
I think not.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is an interesting point. Of course, it is not in my department.

I agree with the minister to this extent, that so long as our law stands as it is, the international agreement precludes our acting in this matter. But my argument in 1935 was, as it is to-day, that we should review the whole situation with a view to modifying our law in order to rectify the matter.
Before I left the department as its minister, I suggested that we should have the national research council make a complete survey, judicial if you like, of the patents held in Canada to-day. A great many patents are held that are not used, but the public do not know this. After all, the most sacred right is the preservation to the inventor of the benefits of his patent; that is the one underlying principle. But the public are entitled to have these inventions used; and if they are not used by the holder of the patent, then, under our law, if the fact is drawn to the attention of the commissioner, the patent may be declared open. Therefore there should be a careful examination by an expert body, and I believe that the national research council is the proper body. A survey would take a long time, but it should be made.
Let me add this-because I am treading on rather delicate ground. I am not for a moment advocating anything that would in any way impinge upon the right of the owner of the patent with respect to his royalty. I do not wish to call in question unduly the corporations concerned, but in so far as there

I am not at all critical of the government, because I know the difficulty and the complexity of the matter, but we should look very carefully into this phase of it.

People are just beginning to realize the value of refrigeration in the home, and we should make it as easy as possible for farmers particularly and people living in the country to get this equipment; they have more need for home refrigeration than people living in the city. When the industry is on an export basis; it is an indication that the tariff is high enough. There is a case here for a reduction from the twenty-five per cent provided in the agreement.

This particular industry
has had a very rapid expansion in the last few years. For many years it was a struggling industry; it has led to the use of a great deal of hydro-electric power. The protection formerly afforded up to 1935 was forty per cent; then by the treaty of 1935 it was reduced to thirty per cent, and is now further reduced to twenty-five per cent.

subtopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OP DETERMINATE FOR INDETERMINATE REFORMATORY SENTENCES

speechtext:
Mr. T. L. CHURCH (Broadview) moved the second reading of Bill No. 12, to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the object of the proposed bill is to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act. This Bill No. 12 is described as "An Act to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act," and starts out in this way:
His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada enacts as follows.
And then follows section 1 of the bill headed "determinate sentences only." It substitutes the old law of the determinate sentence for the indeterminate sentence.
Since the British North America Act and confederation provincial courts have imposed imprisonment for one year and three hundred and sixty-four days. For a great many years that was the law, until the passing of the indeterminate clauses.
The Prisons and Reformatories Act gave the courts jurisdiction to impose an indeterminate term in a reformatory. The bill proposes to substitute a determinate for an indeterminate sentence. The several expressions relating to "indeterminate sentences" are found in eighteen sections or subsections of the act, and the draftsman considers it inexpedient to amend each of such sections by a separate clause. This bill would revert to the old law of sentences for a definite period only. The indeterminate legislation has been condemned by many judges and magistrates as inhuman and illegal.
Canada's prisons at present are filled with youth, many first offenders, who have been unable to secure work. The lack of employment for youth and of a proper national apprenticeship system, by cause and effect is one of the main reasons for crime. Recently the appellate division of the supreme court of Ontario questioned the legality of suoh legislation, because the provinces had the right of providing confinement for only one year and three hundred and sixty-four days, and also condemned the legislation on grounds

2120	COMMONS
Reformatories-Determinate Sentences
of public policy. The law has not acted as a deterrent, nor is it reformative. It should be repealed, because in practice it confers on officials of these institutions the right to detain those who have not influence enough to have employment awaiting them at the end of a definite period, and gives to their decisions the force of statute law.
The effect of these clauses respecting indeterminate sentences is to remove a certain amount of jurisdiction from the courts and to place it in the hands of officials of these institutions, and the parole board. Following judgment in a case Mr. Justice Middleton made some comments, and the attorney general's department circularized the county judges and magistrates advising them to retain a reasonable relationship between determinate and indeterminate sentences.
The royal commission concluded that with the probation system and a central board to administer the ticket-of-leave regulations, the statutory provision for indeterminate sentences might be repealed. On more than one occasion the attorney general for Ontario has intimated his desire to see justice done. May I say that the particular judgment to which I referred is Rex v. Bond, as delivered by the court of appeal. In giving judgment on April 16, 1937, as reported in the Ontario Reports, Mr. Justice Middleton said that the accused was charged with two offences, and pleaded guilty. On each charge the magistrate sentenced him to two years less one day, and an indeterminate term thereafter not to exceed two years, less one day.
Out of the Rex v. Bond judgment I did, when introducing the bill, quote three or four paragraphs. Judge Middleton said that the criminal code, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 36, defines various crimes and, speaking generally, fixes the maximum punishment that may be awarded, but makes, except in a few instances, no provision for the minimum. He said:
In 1916, parliament determined to adopt, so far as the province of Ontario is concerned, the system of indeterminate sentences, and, instead of making an amendment to the code dealing with the matter, passed a statute which is snugly tucked away in the dusty recesses of the Prisons and Reformatories Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, chapter 163, section 46. This section provides "Every court in the province of Ontario, before which any person is convicted for an offence against the laws of Canada, punishable by imprisonment in the common gaol for a term of three months, or for a longer time, may sentence such person to imprisonment for a term of not less than three months and for an indeterminate period thereafter of not more than two years less one day in the Ontario reformatory instead of the common gaol."

This section, it will be observed, is a departure from the fundamental idea that reformatories were for prisoners to be incarcerated for a period of less than two years.
As complementary to this section there is a provision found in section 43 of the same act:
"The lieutenant-governor of the province of Ontario may appoint a board of parole for the said province whose duty it shall be to inquire from time to time into the cases of prisoners sentenced to the Ontario reformatory. . . . And where as a result of such inquiry the board thinks proper it may permit prisoners serving indeterminate sentences to be paroled under conditions approved of by the Minister of Justice and when the terms on which such prisoners have been paroled have been complied with, the board may recommend for the consideration of the Minister of Justice the final discharge of such prisoners."
When I was speaking on Saturday last to one of the ablest crown attorneys, he told me that a great many magistrates in the province do not thoroughly understand the indeterminate sentence. He believes the judgment to which I have referred has a great deal of merit in it. I shall read two further clauses in which the learned judge said:
Many judges and magistrates when imposing an indeterminate sentence address the prisoner somewhat in these terms. . . . "If during this determinate term you prove yourself to be a good prisoner, and comply with the rules of the institution and show a disposition to be law-abiding, the parole board may, at the expiry of the definite term, allow you your liberty. It all depends upon yourself and your conduct as to how much, if any, of the indefinite term you may be called upon to serve."
Thus encouraged, the prisoner proves to be a model prisoner. He gives every indication of his reformation, and is taken at the expiry of the definite term before the board. He is hopeful of liberty and full of good resolutions, and the board announces that by reason of an earlier conviction, a fact well known to the judge who imposed the sentence, they will not allow' him parole, and he must serve the indefinite term. I can imagine no situation more cruel and more likely to convert a man really desiring to reform into an enemy of society.
Indeterminate sentences had their origin in Michigan, and have been adopted in many places. Fundamentally reformatories are for up to one year and three hundred and sixty-four days definite, and by being indeterminate are made four years. The legality of the whole thing is questioned and the court of appeal makes criticisms on its usefulness.
I believe that in these days, when institutions are filled with so many young people, we must take special consideration of the circumstances. We should have law reform all along the line and a Borstal system. I have before me from the bureau of statistics some figures on criminal statistics in Canada. They are issued under the authority of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler). There is reference to the great increase in crime by young people since the depression

Reformatories-Determinate Sentences
began, and it mentions the increased numbers of youthful offenders in all the courts. It also refers to causes and effects. I shall not go into the blue-book tables in detail, because that course, although the figures are most relevant, may not be advisable here on account of time. I may point out briefly, however, that the high prison population is to a large extent the result of unemployment of first offenders, lack of law reform and the sending of too many youths to gaol by magistrates.
Two such youths may get into trouble and appear before the magistrate. The magistrate may fine each ten dollars and costs. One boy's father can pay; but the other boy cannot pay, and as a result there is imprisonment for debt and no way to pay the fine by instalments as I suggested in 1937. That takes place under the system of determinate and indeterminate sentences. Imprisonment for debt was supposed to have been abolished in England in 1864. It is still in vogue in Canada.	[DOT]
I did introduce an amendment in 1937 on behalf of those youthful offenders. My amendment was fashioned after the law in England, known as the Money Payments Procedure Act, 1935, 25 and 26 George V, chapter 46. This was modern, useful legislation, adapted to Canada, and closed many prisons in England, but the minister did not see fit to adopt it, probably on account of his belief that there would be conflict in jurisdiction between the dominion and the provinces, because we are away behind in law reform.
The annual report of the inspector of prisons of the province of Ontario agrees with the federal report in regard to the large number of these youthful offenders. I received many letters from people who have suffered because of the indeterminate and inhuman provisions of this act. One is from an offender whose name I shall not give, but whose number is 21570 at the industrial farm. He says:
Theoretically all men who receive an indefinite sentence have an equal chance of being paroled for the indefinite period of their sentence but in practice this does not seem to work out, seventy-five per cent of those who have indefinite sentences are obliged to serve both the definite and indefinite terms.
The second man, who was sentenced by Magistrate Jones at Toronto, says that he appeared before the parole board, but they refused to' take any action. Parliament has turned over to this board many of its powers and prerogatives. This was never the intention of the fathers of confederation.
I should like to quote from a letter which I received from the attorney general of 71492-134J
Manitoba, Hon. W. J. Major, re this bill of mine. Under date of February 6, 1939, he says:
I find, however, that you and I have approached the problem from different angles. Your quarrel appears to be with the indeterminate sentence; mine is with the determinate sentence. I have taken the position, and so expressed my views in my brief to the penitentiaries commission (copy of which I enclose) that the most reasonably effective method in dealing with the reformation of juvenile delinquents is to permit the imposition of a modified indeterminate sentence with a maximum of three years, and to omit entirely all reference to determinate sentence.
I think after consideration you will conclude that the reason is obvious. When a juvenile is faced with a determinate sentence of two years to be subsequently followed with an indeterminate term the efforts toward reformation will not begin for some period after his incarceration, if at all. He realizes that he must serve two years, with the prospect of further detention.
He argues in favour of the indeterminate sentence, but I think it would be a hardship and inhuman and not in the public interest to put anyone into an institution under such a sentence system. It would not be in the interests of public safety, nor would it be in the interests of the public generally, or of law reform. It would require more prisons than ever, while in England they have closed up half their prisons because of the liberal interpretation they have given to the law, by wise and humane reforms, and by the institution of a national apprenticeship system and national service for youth.
I could read from other letters which I have received, but I do not think I shall say anything more this evening. However, there is one point I should like to bring up. There should also be much greater care taken in the appointment of judges and magistrates. You cannot learn to be a police magistrate in a day. Colonel Denison was a great and humane police magistrate in Toronto for thirty-eight years, and he introduced many wise and modern reforms. He did not have any assistance of outside commissions and new duplicate courts in carrying out the duties of his court. When a family or the husband and wife came to him in trouble, he would advise the wife to go home and cook her husband some good meals, and not both to get cross at the same time. He gave good advice to many youthful offenders. He was always very careful as to whom he sent to prison, not as is the case now in dealing with first offenders in trouble from distress and lack of work.
To-day a man is sent to prison simply because he has no money. One boy comes up before a court, and because he is well off
2122	COMMONS
Reformatories-Determinate Sentences
he is able to pay the ten dollars he is fined. Another boy is too poor to raise the fine and he goes to gaol. There should be more care taken in making these judicial appointments and in deciding who is to be sent to these institutions. We are twenty-five years behind England in these law reforms, as the prison reports of England show. I do hope there will be a study made of this particular system. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation (Mr. Woodsworth) has taken an interest in this work in Winnipeg. I do not think it would be in the interests of justice to have indeterminate sentences instead of determinate. A man would not know when he was going to get out. Perhaps that would be all right if the officials in these institutions were properly trained. Notwithstanding what the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) said the other evening, there are hundreds of these young people riding the rods. They get into trouble, and they receive determinate plus indeterminate sentences.
I am sorry that I have not been able to find a long letter which I received some years ago from the late Chief Justice R. M. Meredith at the time when the indeterminate sentence legislation had been in force for years. It was either shortly before or shortly after he retired that he wrote me this long letter in which he gave his views of the indeterminate sentence. He contended that such sentences were illegal under the British North America Act and under the code and against public policy. He was very much against them. He was out on circuit for thirty-eight years, and I believe he tried more cases than probably any other judge we ever had in the province in the supreme court. He was strongly opposed to the principle of indeterminate sentences as inhuman and unreformative. This principle has also been condemned by the court of appeal, as I have already shown.
In these days when so many young people are getting into trouble, instead of bringing about reforms and providing education we are doing the exact opposite. The result is that many men are sent to these institutions for committing the most trivial offences. There is an injustice on the families as well. I should like to quote from a report as to the number of inmates in the Toronto gaol. I did not note in the press report the date. I lost it. Governor Denning reports to the city hall:
There were 295 inmates in the gaol last night, nearly an all-time record. Out of this total 275 were men and 20 women. All cells were occupied. Cots had to be placed in the corridors. The normal limit at the gaol is 230; that is what the gaol can accommodate.

After that it is up to the governor and his staff to figure out how to "bed down" tbe prisoners and look after the discipline.
Those may not be the exact figures for to-day, and this condition may not apply all over the province. The commission which recently sat found many of our provincial institutions had been built before confederation and against all the known laws of hygiene. I think we should follow the example of England where they have closed up half the prisons, and have some modem prison reform.

subtopic: PROPOSED SUBSTITUTION OP DETERMINATE FOR INDETERMINATE REFORMATORY SENTENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the express
object of this bill is to eliminate the power to impose indeterminate sentences in Ontario under the Prisons and Reformatories Act. Section 46 of that act authorizes the courts of Ontario to impose upon any person convicted for an offence punishable by imprisonment in the common gaol a term of three months' determinate and an indeterminate period thereafter of not more than two years less one day in the Ontario reformatory instead of the common gaol. Under section 43 of the act the Ontario board of parole is instituted whose duty is to inquire into the cases of prisoners sentenced to certain institutions. After such inquiry the board may permit certain prisoners serving indeterminate sentences to be paroled under conditions approved by the Minister of Justice.
The section continues:	[DOT]
.	.	. and when the terms on which such
prisoners have been paroled have been complied with, the board may recommend for the consideration of the Minister of Justice the final discharge of such prisoners.
The question of the indeterminate sentence was studied by the royal commission appointed to investigate penitentiaries and to study penal reform in general, and in their report they devote a few pages to this question. They mention that there have been some difficulties in Ontario because of a certain conflict between some of the magistrates and the board of parole, which led to the decision in the appeal court to which my hon. friend has referred. That decision is also mentioned in the report of the royal commission. I think for the better understanding of this question I might be permitted to read just a few sentences from that part of their report which the commissioners devote to this question. After commenting upon that decision of the appeal court they say, at page 247 :[DOT]
Your commissioners are of the opinion that if indeterminate sentences are to be continued in the province of Ontario there should not be such conflict between the board of parole and the judges and magistrates in tbe province. It is clear that judges and magistrates should not sentence prisoners to the Ontario refor-

Reformatories-Determinate Sentences
matory for indeterminate periods when, having regard to the prisoner's previous record and his opportunities for reform, it is clear that he is not likely to be a good subject for parole at the end of the determinate period. As has been pointed out, the success of a prisoner on parole does not depend on his behaviour in prison, but on his will and determination to conform to the laws of the country and the conventions of society and on the likelihood of his carrying out that determination under proper supervision.
The efforts of the authorities who are in charge of the reformatories in Ontario are greatly handicapped by the practice of sentencing incorrigible criminals to the reformatories, by means of imposing indeterminate sentences, for longer periods than would otherwise be justifiable under the act. Mr. Neelands drew the attention of your commission to one case in which a prisoner was sentenced to the reformatory for terms of two years less one day determinate plus two years less a day indeterminate on each of two charges which were to run consecutively, with the result that the prisoner wras required to serve a term in the reformatory of eight years less four days. Your commissioners are of the opinion that this was not the intention of parliament when the legislation was enacted.
Following the judgment of the court of appeal in May; 1937, Mr. I. A. Humphries, K.C., the deputy attorney general for the province of Ontario, sent out a circular letter to all magistrates and county judges, enclosing a copy of the "Reasons for Judgment" of the court of appeal, and adding certain observations thereon. These observations may be summarized as follows:
1.	The period of the indeterminate sentence should bear some relation to the period of the determinate sentence. For instance, a definite sentence of three months should not be followed by an indeterminate sentence of two years less a day;
2.	Consecutive indeterminate sentences should not be given;
3.	In no case should the court state to the prisoner what the action of the board of parole may be, or the considerations which may impel the board of parole to release the prisoner.
It appears that this letter has had some effect in correcting the situation that had previously existed in respect to indeterminate sentences.
Your commissioners are of the opinion that, if the recommendations of this commission are adopted in respect to the establishment of an adult probation system, and a central parole board is established to administer the Tieket-of-Leave Act, with adequate investigation and supervision in the provinces and an adequate system for the treatment of young offenders in the prisons, the present statutory provision for indeterminate sentences in Ontario might be repealed.
So this recommendation, is subject to certain other improvements that would first have to be made before we would do away with the system which has prevailed in Ontario for such a long time. The commission which will be appointed will have to study the various aspects of this question, and until this is done I would not favour any amendment to the Prisons and Reformatories Act
so far as the indeterminate sentence is concerned.
I may say, and my hon. friend has shown it himself, that opinion is far from being unanimous on this question. As a matter of fact, at the time my hon. friend was introducing his bill to do away with indeterminate sentences, the attorney general of Manitoba was asking the Department of Justice to change the criminal code so as to do away with determinate sentences. As my hon. friend said, he and the attorney general of Manitoba are perhaps trying to reach the same goal, but they view it from a different angle. He wants to abolish the indeterminate sentence, and Mr. Major wants to abolish the determinate sentence. I have here the letter of the attorney general of Manitoba, but I suppose it is not necessary to read it and put it on Hansard. Indeed, he rather asks my hon. friend to change his bill altogether and substitute the abolition of determinate sentences rather than the indeterminate.
With respect to the wording of the bill, I do not think it would accomplish satisfactorily the object which my hon. friend seeks to accomplish. For instance, his bill merely says that whenever the expression, "an indeterminate sentence" or "an indeterminate period" is found in any one of the sections which he mentions in his bill it should be replaced by the expression "determinate term." So, under section 43, which gives to the parole board of Ontario certain powers with respect to indeterminate sentences, if you changed indeterminate to determinate sentences, you would be clothing the parole board of Ontario with powers which are really under the Minister of Justice with regard to remission or mercy in all cases of determinate sentences.
For these reasons I believe this bill cannot be adopted at this time more particularly, and even if it had more merits than I am able to find in it, I would say that it is premature and my hon. friend should wait until such changes as are suggested by the royal commission can be studied.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. J. S. Woodsworth (Winnipeg North Centre) for the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the criminal code.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the debate on the second reading of this bill was adjourned, I was attempting to show the necessity of the federal enactment which is now proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). I was also pointing out how powerful corporations may defeat the rights of workers to organize and bargain collectively, and was using as an illustration the experience of the strike at Blubber Bay, in British Columbia.
The purpose of the bill, as explained, is to prevent employers from refusing to employ, or from dismissing employees, or conspiring with others therefor, for the reason that they are members of a trade union. It was pointed out that it was lawful for workmen or employees to form themselves into trades unions and bargain collectively; that therefore, as a matter of public policy, it should be unlawful for employers to seek by overt acts of intimidation, threats or conspiracy, to prevent their employees from belonging to such trade unions. Throughout the years organized workers have by dint of great struggle attempted to build up their rights to organize. A fundamental right of civil liberty is the right to organize, the right to bargain collectively. Their rights in this respect are not clearly defined, and under circumstances which prevail in some parts of Canada it does become readily possible for powerful corporations to invoke the law resulting in severe penalties to organized workers if they attempt to assert their rights, or where police forces are susceptible to influence, to use the law enforcement agencies to defeat their purposes in attempting to bargain collectively.

In British Columbia we have an act known as the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act. I mention that because the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) last session made a special point of stating that in all the provinces adequate legislation existed to deal with the question, and therefore it should be left exclusively to the jurisdiction of the provincial authority. He also claimed that it would be inadvisable to make it a crime for employers to act in this way. May I point out that frequently, because of the lawful efforts of organized workers to assert their rights, and because of lawless efforts on the part of the employers who are not restrained under the criminal code from such activities, serious situations result such as that to which I am about to refer.
British Columbia provides, under the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act, that it shall be lawful for employees to bargain collectively with their employers and to conduct such bargaining through representatives of the employees duly elected by a majority of the employees affected, and any employer or employers refusing so to bargain shall be liable to a fine not exceeding S500 for each offence. An attempt has been made in British Columbia to enforce that act, and on one occasion we had the amazing declaration made by the minister of labour of British Columbia that it would be impossible for him to enforce this act against a powerful corporation because unquestionably they would carry the matter on appeal to the privy council and make it extremely awkward for the provincial government.
The situation to which I refer specifically, the strike at Blubber Bay, was with regard to the operations of the Pacific Lime Company, a company controlling practically the only payroll on Texada island, an isolated spot. Comparatively few men were involved, but the strike assumed importance because of the proximity of other unions on the mainland at Powell River and of the miners' organizations on Vancouver island. All these organizations have been extremely interested in the strike at Blubber Bay and in the policies disclosed with regard to the attempted settlement of the strike.
Approximately 150 men are employed in quarrying operations. The company quarries limestone and has control over practically the only source of high-class lime on the Pacific coast. Working conditions for some time were unsatisfactory. The men made some attempt to organize during 1937, and several disputes ensued. Finally, in September, 1937, a definite agreement was reached between the employees and the company as

Criminal Code-Trade Unions
a result of organization, and this agreement is the one I have in my hand. It reads in part as follows:
This company agrees to bargain collectively with its own employees through a committee elected by the employees as a whole; it being understood that the company does not recognize any affiliation between its employees and any outside union.
The company also agrees that no discrimination shall be shown against any employee by reason of the strike declared on July 23, 1937.
The agreement then proceeds to outline increases of pay and pay for overtime, and concludes with the sentence that:
Either party to this agreement desiring to terminate same shall notify the other party in writing thirty days in advance of termination.
In addition to this agreement, certain practices were followed at Blubber Bay, and particularly with regard to the employment of men laid off during the slack period. During slack periods the work was rotated in a fashion; the men remained in the district, and if available were reengaged when the work increased. But after the attempt was made to organize, and even after this agreement was reached, it is, I think, now a matter of record that the company violated almost every article of the agreement made with the men. As a matter of fact, only four days after the agreement was signed they disregarded the understanding with regard to boat loading, and they also employed new men for drilling operations, although the old-time employees, men experienced in the work of drilling, were on hand. The union then formed found it necessary to threaten a strike in order to maintain satisfactory working conditions in that regard. But the company made a special point of refusing to reengage men who had been active in the union, and imported from Vancouver men who had not been in the employ of the company. May I add just at this point that the average term of employment of the employees was approximately fourteen years.
In January following this agreement the company actually called together a meeting of its employees and attempted to exercise influence to have them declare themselves against the International Wood Workers of America, an international organization with which the union was affiliated. Three members of the International Wood Workers' Association were actually at one stage excluded from the meeting by the activities of the company. Finally the men voted ten to one for the union committee, and, following the meeting, ninety-two signatures were obtained on a petition to the minister of labour of the province. The petition asked that a conciliator be sent in to deal with the various matters
in dispute. On February 12, 1938, a commissioner under the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act was sent in with Mr. Moriarty, as interpreter, and a meeting was held between the employers and the employees. A secret ballot was taken to determine their method of representation, making it clear that the employees should have the right to select a union of their own choice. Two slates, one named by union and the other by non-union men, were submitted to the employees. They voted eighty-seven to thirty in favour of a union committee. The conciliator, Mr. Mc-Geogh, ruled in favour of the men and ordered the company to meet with the committee elected by the men. However, when that committee approached the company the company flatly refused to negotiate and notified the committee that in future the company would hire all men from Vancouver.
That was an exceedingly serious matter because any man who could not secure employment with the Pacific Lime Company would be virtually compelled to leave Texada island inasmuch as there were no other forms of employment available to him there. Again the organized employees applied for a conciliator under the provincial act. I emphasize the fact that the employees who were in dispute with the company followed step by step every legal process open to them under the provincial law. Before the conciliator arrived, the company again indulged in discriminatory practices, and the men went on strike on March 6, at the same time presenting their grievances to the company. Again two commissioners arrived at this point and persuaded the company to open negotiations on condition that the men returned to work. The men returned to work on March 12. The committees and officials of the company met in negotiation, but a deadlock soon took place, following which the men made application for an arbitration board as provided under the arbitration act. Even then, during the month of April, 1938, while the government of British Columbia was taking steps to set up an arbitration board, the Pacific Lime Company discharged nine of their regular employees, for no other reason apparently than that they had engaged in the organization of a union, and filled their places with men recruited from recipients of relief in the adjacent districts.
Here I pause to stress the fact that these men were recruited through the agency of the provincial police of British Columbia from the area known as the Sechelt peninsula. Men who were on relief, it is declared in affidavits, were told that if they did not accept strikebreaking duty at Blubber Bay their relief
Criminal Code-Trade Unions

would be cut off. A number of affidavits were produced to that effect. As a result of these practices the employees again quit work and appealed to the minister of labour of British Columbia, who instructed the company to reinstate the men or face prosecution under the act. In the arbitration proceedings which followed, Mr. Harold Winch, M.L.A., represented the men before the board of arbitration and produced a letter which had been circulated among the men by their employers urging them against belonging to an affiliate of the C.I.O. Counsel for the company stated that this organization was not a Canadian union but was controlled in the United States and that its reputation was not such as to inspire the company with confidence, thereby making it clear that the company intended to deny the men the right to select a union of their own choice. There are innumerable instances of anti-union activities on the part of the company, and there was continual discrimination, which resulted in the application for the board of arbitration.
Mr. Justice McIntosh was chairman of the board, the other members being Mr. Frank Leigh, and Mr. R. D. Williams, designated by the lieutenant governor in council. The board held sessions at Blubber Bay on May 4 and 5, and on May 10 handed down a unanimous report. The Pacific Lime Company notified the department of labour of British Columbia that they would accept the award. I have here a copy of the award. Several sections were in dispute as being ultra vires of the Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act, a section of which requires the employer to recognize a committee elected by a majority of the employees. At the request of Mr. Pearson, provincial minister of labour, Mr. Justice McIntosh returned to Blubber Bay and dealt with these difficulties to the satisfaction of the company and the men.
One of the principal clauses of the award was that the company should reinstate the men who had been black listed, if those men were available and as opportunity should arise. The meeting following the second session of the arbitration board proceeded to work out plans for the implementing of the terms of the award. The chief point was the reinstatement of twenty-three men who had been black listed by the Pacific Lime Company. Although the company professed their willingness to accept the amended award, they definitely refused to work out a plan for the reinstatement of the twenty-three men who had been black listed. They refused to declare when they would reinstate the men, or to set a time limit, or to suggest any procedure that would be followed with a view

to reinstating them. They said that they would have to consider their so-called loyal employees, that is, the men brought in, in the weeks immediately preceding, to take the place of the men who had been black listed because of trade union activities.
Mr. Justice McIntosh did not spare the company in his remarks, particularly in regard to their stand on behalf of the so-called loyal employees. He said definitely that they "should go down to the mill in the morning and dismiss those men." He emphasized that the men were brought in during the dispute and said that he would not be in the least surprised if they were dismissed, and he pressed the company to reinstate the twenty-three men round whom the dispute centred and who had been loyal to the company for terms of employment ranging up to thirty years. The company refused to make terms of reinstatement, but stated quite defiantly to the government and to the men that they would not reinstate them; and after waiting several weeks the men struck on June 2, 1938. As far as I am aware, that strike is still in progress.
Since the strike was declared the authorities in British Columbia made several earnest endeavours to settle the dispute. For several very good reasons there is still danger that certain business will be tied up if the unions in the United States handling cargoes take a sympathetic point of view. Sympathetic action on the part of affiliated trade unions would seriously disrupt business operations in British Columbia.

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext: The hon. member mentioned twenty-three men who were dismissed. Were any of the old employees retained?

subtopic: PROVISION AGAINST REFUSAL TO EMPLOY OR DISMISSAL FOR MEMBERSHIP IN TRADE UNIONS
speechtext:
Yes, I believe there were; but I am referring to the men who formed themselves into a union and attempted to secure recognition of that union by the company, and who were black listed and dismissed1; none of those men was reinstated. Mr. John Stanton, barrister of Vancouver, made a splendid effort to bring the company and the men together. Mr. Colin Cameron, M.L.A., Mr. Harold Winch, M.L.A., and many other individuals approached the company, and eventually Mr. Justice McIntosh again went to the company, urged the courts to adjourn the various trials, and attempted to reach some settlement. The company refused to reinstate the men. At first they promised they would reinstate six or seven or eight of them; subsequent negotiations revealed their willingness to reinstate the majority of the white men but not any of the orientals involved, who had given long and faithful service.

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
To every attempt made by the provincial government during or subsequently to the arbitration proceedings the company took a defiant attitude and evinced determination to crush the strike.
When the strike was called, a detachment of the provincial police was sent to Blubber Bay, and it is to the disgrace of British Columbia that this police force was used to intimidate the strikers and provoke them to disorder. The employees were men known to be industrious and law-abiding, but they were subjected to what I consider to be acts of terrorism. There was a lady in the community, whose house had been built by public subscription when her husband died in the employ of the plant and whose house was not on the company property; an attempt was made forcibly to evict her, in the presence of the police officers. Affidavits were made showing that attempts were made to suborn witnesses to give perjured evidence that money was obtained by methods of extortion, without the man being formally charged or appearing before a magistrate. There was deliberate provocation by the police, until a large number of charges of unlawful assembly resulted. Men were arrested on various pretexts. I well remember that for a whole Sunday men crazed with liquor ran wild in Blubber Bay, intimidating and in some instances actually assaulting innocent persons, and the police standing by offered no protection to those who sympathized with the strikers. I was present on one occasion when a barrister of repute made an affidavit in the presence of the attorney general of British Columbia to the effect that the magistrate sitting on one of these cases had been under the influence of liquor when dealing with the case. The whole matter was such as to undermine confidence in the administration of law and order in that section of British Columbia, and it resulted from the deliberate and determined efforts of a well entrenched company to deny a legitimate union the right to conduct its legitimate activities.
The situation became so serious that one police officer was finally charged with assault, convicted and sentenced to six months' imprisonment. The offence which he committed was that he did assault a man arrested on a charge of unlawful assembly after that man had been placed in the house used by the police detachment for their purposes. That man was seriously injured, and although sentenced on the charge of unlawful assembly was at the point of death for many months, as a result of these injuries.

speechtext: Was that the municipal police?
