speechtext:
A provincial police officer, a member of the detachment especially imported to Blubber Bay on strike duty, who,
I say, took no pains to conceal their desire to take the part of the company and smash the strike. A few level-headed police officers on the scene might have made it clear that they were there to protect property and maintain law and order, and might have avoided all the serious trouble which resulted. The courts were clogged with charges of assault, unlawful assembly and rioting for many months afterwards, and this caused grave concern to citizens of British Columbia interested in the maintenance of law and order. The law was brought into ridicule because of the actions of some police officers sent to Blubber Bay on strike duty.
While I cannot now go into more details of a very sad chapter in the industrial history of British Columbia, I suggest to the Minister of Justice that it is a crime for employers to do what was done in Blubber Bay. They used the power which is theirs to intimidate employees and prevent legitimate trade union activity; they found it possible to influence law enforcement in British Columbia in order to place the strikers at a disadvantage, and where you have officers susceptible to that kind of influence it is very easy to charge that any assembly, such as a picket line, is an unlawful assembly, threatening or presumed to threaten a disturbance of the peace. The law was brought into contempt in British Columbia 'by reason of that action with sad results, which will leave a deep impression in the minds of citizens of British Columbia for many years to come. I suggest it is now high time that we make definite provision in the criminal code of Canada declaring it to be unlawful for employers to intimidate in that fashion employees who are attempting legitimately to bargain for their rights.
On motion of Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) the debate was adjourned.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.

speechtext: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved the third reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
When this bill was up for second reading and during the committee stage I discussed it at some length. I shall endeavour not to traverse
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

again the ground that I covered on those two occasions, but to state briefly some reasons why I consider this legislation to be of a retrograde character.
Over a long period of years there have been developed in the legislation of Canada certain safeguards to control the expenditure of public money. As a result of long experience certain principles have been adopted to ensure this control.
This is a bill to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which originally was passed in 1935 as an emergency measure. The original legislation was of this nature: There had been an area in Saskatchewan and Alberta and the western section of Manitoba subjected to drought for several years; there was soil drifting, and the -farmers in -this district were suffering. It was found advisable for parliament to pass certain legislation enabling a study to be made of the situation. So a bill was passed authorizing the appointment of a representative committee. I read the details of that clause on the second reading. This committee was of an advisory character to advise the minister as to what measures might be taken to rehabilitate the area. That, as I say, was in 1935.
In 1937 the act was amended, broadening its character. It must be borne in mind-and I wish it had been possible for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to have been present to-night, because I consider this is a matter of rather unusual importance-that the original measure provided for examination into the situation, and for certain emergency measures. But it limited the amount of expenditure in the act itself, and provided for other safeguards and limitations.
In the act of 1937 the original act was amended and the groundwork somewhat broadened. The 1937 bill really erects what was originally passed as an emergency measure into an important piece of permanent legislation. It may be questioned as to whether or not it is permanent. But when I point out that in his elucidation of the works which had already been undertaken and brought into operation the minister stated last night that some of it was constructed to last for at least twenty years, the permanency will be realized.
I think in regard to many of the operations he would not limit it to that time.
Furthermore,' thousands of acres, tens of thousands, yes, hundreds of thousands of acres of land have been and are being purchased, which erects the whole undertaking as a permanent structure. For instance, when speaking last night the minister gave certain information, some of which I shall quote. He apparently impressed the house with the significance 
of what the government is doing. For example, he referred to Caron water storage, at a cost of $400,000; Cypress lake storage, at a cost of $304,696.13; Downie lake irrigation project at a cost of $61,461.65; the Brooks irrigation project extending over an area of 25,000 acres, the Eastend extension at a cost of $30,661.45; the Glen Ewen dam storage at a cost of S9.471.40; the Kisbey Flats irrigation project costing $23,121.50; the Pipestone lake storage, costing $7,523.25; the Oxbow-Souris river storage dam at a cost of $16,130; the Souris-Estevan irrigation project at a cost of $52,903.86; the South Saskatchewan river storage project at a cost of $243,106.25; the west Valmarie irrigation project at a cost of $43,987.50; the Weyburn rural municipality underground storage -project, costing $3,333,33, and the Leavitt irrigation district project, to cost $46,304.80.
These are the works with which we are dealing in this legislation. And I may say that, in addition to these, there are about 5,000 individual, smaller operations.

That saves me the trouble of looking it up.
The only point I make is that this constitutes a permanent undertaking. It is not something which is any longer of an emergency nature. My complaint is that m this legislation before the house we are giving to the minister powers which over the years have gradually been taken away from ministerial control, not through any reflection upon ministers, but as a matter of experience and to safeguard the proper control of public
expenditures.
As an illustration let me turn to the Department of Transport Stores Act, 1937. There we find this safeguard:
All transactions affecting the accounts herein provided for shall be subject to all the . provisions and regulations of The Consolidated Revenue and Audit Act 1931, except as otherwise herein provided.
That is one safeguard not found in this
legislation.
Then, the Public Works Construction Act was somewhat similar to the measure now under consideration. It, too, was emergency legislation. Let us remember that in connection with these undertakings for the irrigation of land, valuable areas of land are to be acquired. Under this measure, subject to the approval of the governor in council, we empower the minister to acquire lands, and so on. But in the Public Works Construction Act, section 3 we find this:
The governor in council may acquire such lands as may be necessary for the purposes of this act and the provisions of the Expropriation Act, chapter 64 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927, shall apply.
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
I am not saying that in every instance the Expropriation Act should apply, but I do submit it would be advisable to have the acquisition of land under this legislation subject to the Expropriation Act or, in cases where the Expropriation Act were not considered necessary, the governor in council should make special provision for it.
Another point is this:	It is not obligatory
upon the minister to call for tenders. On the other hand, under the Public Works Construction Act it is obligatory upon the minister to call for tenders, and the provision reads as follows:
Except as hereinafter provided the minister or department of the government entrusted with the administration, management and execution of any of the works set forth in schedule A to this act shall invite tenders for the construction and execution of such works, and contracts for all such works and undertakings shall be awarded under the direction of the governor in council.
I submit that also should be included in this bill. Another provision which should be included is to be found in the Public Works Construction Act, 1935. This reads:
All orders in council made under the provisions of this act shall be laid before the House of Commons forthwith after the making thereof if parliament is then sitting, and if not, then said orders in council or an abstract thereof disclosing their essential provisions shall be published in the next following issue of the Canada Qazette and laid before parliament in the case of all expenditures the amounts of which are not specifically set forth in schedule A to this act within the first fifteen days of the next ensuing session.
The reason for that provision in that act was similar to the reason why a similar provision should be included in this legislation. The new section 12 empowers the minister to dispose of equipment; in fact, under that section he can dispose of a great many things. I did not attempt to look up the records, but I have referred to the Public Works Act, which is chapter 166 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. This is a very old statute, and I cite it because it shows that for years parliament has carefully guarded this sort of thing. Section 39 of that act reads:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, or in any other act contained, any public work not required for public purposes may be sold or leased, under the authority of the governor in council; and the proceeds of such sale or lease shall be accounted for as public moneys: Provided that such public work shall be so sold or leased by tender or at auction after public advertisement.
And so on. The reason why I refer to that is the fact that yesterday it was suggested to the minister that these articles should be disposed of by public auction. There is a wide range of activities authorized under this
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

bill. It is impossible for the minister personally to keep in contact with several thousand undertakings. When I say several thousand, I am not exaggerating because the report which was tabled, which is incomplete, shows that applications have been made for over
11,000,	and the projects reported completed number 4,588. That was a year ago, and during 1938 several thousand more have been added. It is obviously impossible for the minister or the deputy minister to keep in touch with the various projects, and therefore it is doubly desirable that reasonable safeguards should be maintained. I am not asking for anything new, I am simply suggesting that the existing safeguards in connection with the disposal of equipment and property shall be maintained. I think that could be done by adopting in this measure the old, well tried practices of the Department of Transport, which was formerly the Department of Marine, in connection with its stores, and of the Department of Public Works and the other operating departments of the government which through long experience have found the best method of dealing with these matters.
It was not my intention to prolong the debate or delay this matter. I simply wanted to reiterate what I had expressed before, that in my opinion this legislation represents a loosening up of what has long been recognized as the necessary control by parliament over the expenditure of public money. It is a retrograde step. This legislation is making permanent that which was adopted a few years ago under an emergency, and we are doing it with an almost frivolous attitude. We have not worked out a well thought out statute to control this vast undertaking. It is a vast undertaking. It is like having a working government within the government. It has all the potentialities of a Department of Public Works being operated by the Department of Agriculture. This latter department has not the personnel or the training to deal with many of these larger undertakings. I have already referred to irrigation schemes which will run into $300,000 or $400,000. These are to be constructed under the direction of the Department of Agriculture when we have an efficient Department of Public Works which could undertake this work. The small dug-outs and the little local water storage basins could probably be constructed by the Department of Agriculture, but these larger works ought to be under the Department of Public Works, and be supervised by the laws of the country which control expenditures of this kind.
I am quite aware that I shall lay myself open to the suggestion that I am reflecting 
on the minister, but this has nothing to do with him at all. It is purely a non-personal matter. My objection is to the principle of the bill, to the retrograde nature of the legislation and to the at least partial abandonment of the regular safeguards which have been used for many years in this country in connection with such matters.
Mr. KARL K. HOMUTH (Waterloo South): Mr. Speaker, I have had some experience with legislation and with government. One thing which amazes me is the number of measures which are passed through this house empowering ministers to do within their own departments works which should necessarily come under some other department. One almost begins to wonder whether or not this session is just a prelude to a general election when what is so often referred to in the United States as the pork-barrel is opened up for the purposes of an election within a few months. Everything in connection with this bill gives to the minister power which I submit no minister should have. When expenditures such as these are undertaken, I believe that they ought to be undertaken by the department of government which knows something about construction, engineering and the carrying out of such works. We have gone into the motion picture business; we have the Department of National Defence; apparently everything that is being done is subject to the charge of patronage. Surely the time has come when the people of Canada should be sick and tired of political patronage. They are sick and tired of it. I for one want to protest against the putting through of legislation which, like this bill, is going to give the power of political patronage to a minister.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are being asked to approve the third reading of Bill No. 36, to amend the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. The main part of the amendment has to do with an appropriation of $450,000, a large sum of money. The minister may make argeements with the provinces, with municipalities, cities and towns, or with any individual or corporation. That is contrary to the other labour and relief legislation of the government where the municipalities must deal with the provinces.
I think this Bill No. 36 is class legislation of the worst kind. If you are going to assist the prairie provinces on their way to recovery, then by the British North America Act in relation to concurrent jurisdiction in agriculture, there should be equality of treatment for all the other provinces because they have farm problems as well. I was very much

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
surprised at the kind of argument that was used on the second reading of this bill. It was claimed that the prairie provinces had paid St7.000,000 through the tariff over a period of years, and now three or four million dollars a year are to be set aside to assist the prairies because of that new argument. That seems to be the principle on which the minister is going in this bill. I never knew any other minister to accept or adopt such a principle. It is based on a fallacy and unfounded. I never heard such an argument used before in all the parliaments I have sat in until this one.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, this bill is sectional, for the benefit of one part of Canada only at the expense of another. As I said in parliament last year in connection with similar legislation, I cannot understand the policy of this government as it appears in this bill. The policy is all wrong. There was a return brought down to this house for the late Mr. McCrea which showed that so far as agriculture was concerned the jurisdiction under the British North America Act was concurrent between the dominion and the provinces. It never was the intention of the fathers of confederation by the widest stretch of imagination that the principle of federal assistance to the prairies should be carried out along the lines of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and this amendment by Bill No. 36. This is class legislation; it is not in the public interest, and somebody must pay for it. The return to which I referred showed that these millions of dollars of assistance for the prairies came from the industrial provinces of Ontario and Quebec to the extent of eighty per cent. These two provinces pay eighty per cent of all the cash taxes of Canada. Since the present minister has been in charge of this department, he seems to have turned this high court of parliament into a parliament only for the benefit of Saskatchewan at the expense of the rest of Canada.
The argument that the east is getting a subsidy through the tariff is very far-fetched indeed. Hon. gentlemen from the west say that the three prairie provinces have contributed 517,000,000 through the tariff to the east. Where is it? What did that $47,000,000 consist of? It is simply an academic argument, and I never heard it used until the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) came into the house in 1935. It is not an economic or a business argument or even a fact. It sets one section of this country against another. It sets the west against the industrial provinces of the east, against Ontario and against your province, Mr. Speaker, from which sixty-five members come to this parliament looking for similar treatment.
I will give the reasons for the principles of this bill. I stated in the.house last year the reasons for the failure of agriculture on the prairies, and I quoted at that time from an article in the National Review entitled "Waste Not Want Not," which describes conditions on the prairies and in the waste agriculture places of the United States. It says:
There is no country in the world where machinery is utilized more in everyday life than in the United States of America, and there is no country in the world where human and material waste is becoming more evident. The American used the machine to extinguish the amenities of his soil, and he reaps the whirlwind, or the dirt storm. He turned his machines on the timber, and he finds himself confronted with rising waters in the shape of floods, and falling waters in the form of droughts. If he continues on the same lines, employing his ruthless mechanisms on industrial projects without due consideration of wastage of raw materials and wastage in human power, he may conceivably awake like Rip van Winkle in another generation and discover that all the empty gunny sacks in the countryside will not clothe and feed the miserable population.
In the Dominion of Canada the fisheries are a declining factor, consequent on the application of a maximum of mechanical age and a minimum of human power. The prairies in the central regions are losing their fertility in an endeavour to supply wheat for exportation with a maximum of machine power and a minimum of man power; and the same sequence applies to timber or mineral productions. Over eighty per cent of Canada's exportations are basic raw materials, or primary products, and the whole population of this vast extent of the earth's surface is only in the neighbourhood of 11,000,000.
The point which I wish to make clear is that during the last decade since machinery in the dominion has been employed in geometrical progression towards the destruction of primary natural resources for export, the country has failed to increase in man power. Not only is this the case, but the problem of unemployment is probably as acute in Canada as elsewhere. The same reasoning holds to a more or less degree when applied to other parts of the British empire from which countries, dominated by industrialism or unrelentless machine economy, derive their supplies of raw material.
It is no solution of this question of raw materials which contends that if ^ the imperial markets from whence Great Britain obtains her present supplies were thrown open to the world at large under a league of nations or other committee a situation would be created whereby peace would become the stabilized condition of human existence, machine economy and trade the governing factors, and war an outrage.
I contend that if the government of Canada, which has concurrent jurisdiction with the provinces in agriculture, is going to give
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

by this bill federal assistance running into tens of millions of dollars a year to the prairie provinces, then under the British North America Act the farmers of the other provinces are entitled to the very same treatment. Agriculture, as a matter of fact, should have been at confederation a provincial responsibility, with each province looking after its own agriculture; but under sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act the dominion and the provinces have concurrent jurisdiction in agriculture. Is it to be concurrent only for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, or is the concurrency to apply to the other provinces where they have similar problems of drought and poor crops? I say that the other provinces are not going to stand for contributing out of current revenue and out of capital all this federal assistance to one section only of Canada.
Hon. gentlemen argue that the west has contributed 847,000,000 through the tariff, and they contend that the east is subsidized through the tariff. I believe in the only principle of confederation, each for all and all for each, for each of the provinces. If you cany that argument to a legitimate conclusion-although I have never used it before, I have heard it used in a great protectionist paper, the Evening Telegram of Toronto, by a gentleman who was editor for nearly forty years and probably knew more about protection and the tariff in relation to the prairies than some members of the cabinet;
I am not using it; I am' giving it in answer to the argument proposed-it is not. open to hon. gentlemen on my left to say that the industrial provinces have a subsidy of 847,000,000 from the west, because I can tell them this, that the greatest enemy the western farmer has is not east of the great lakes, his greatest enemy as a grain grower is the free trader on the prairies. The free traders are very largely to blame for this trouble on the prairies. They, the elevator combines, the grain exchange and others in the west are responsible largely for the farmers' difficulties because they have tried to make western agriculture a north and south industry instead of an east and west industry. Some of the worst enemies the west had were free traders in Regina and other prairie capitals and cabinet ministers who shared their opinions when they proposed free trade in grain along those lines and when they opposed inquiries into the grain industry, as, for instance, when they secured an injunction in the Maharg case, so preventing a proper inquiry into the evils suffered by the farmers on the prairies from combines and middlemen who handle grain,

I believe in the principle of confederation, each for all and all for each; but I believe the day is not far distant when parliament can no longer make these hand-outs under the British North America Act to the west unless they give the same treatment under the very same act under concurrent jurisdiction to the maritimes, to British Columbia, and to the industrial provinces where, in Ontario and Quebec, are hundreds of farmers in destitute circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
One or two remarks have been made to which I should like to reply. In the first place it has been suggested by one or two of the speakers that this is a rather remarkable piece of legislation. In particular, I believe the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth), in the few observations he made, referred to it as a set-up just prior to a coming election for the purpose of giving patronage. If one looks at the legislation on which these amendments are based, one finds that the legislation was passed by the House of Commons on April 11, 1935, which was just prior to the last federal election, and passed by the government which was then in office; and in spite of the remarks of the hon. member for Waterloo South, who has very lately come into the house, I am not inclined to think the bill was passed by the government of the day for the purpose of giving out patronage in connection with the election which was then in the offing. I am quite sure that members of the house to-day are not at all in agreement with the hon. member for Waterloo South that the present intentions with respect to any legislation that may be brought into the house are for the purpose he indicated.
Bill No. 55, introduced in 1935, is in principle identical with the act which is still on the statute books. This bill deals in very much the same terms as the act which is now on the statute books. In the first place, the first section declares:
In this act and in any regulations made thereunder, unless the context otherwise requires, "minister" means the Minister of Agriculture.
In other words, it was not the present government but the government of our predecessors that placed this particular work under the control of the Department of Agriculture, and it has remained under the control of the Minister of Agriculture from that day to the present time.

Section 3 provides that the governor in council may establish a committee. The only change in that section was made during the session of 1937 when the word "committees" was substituted for the word "committee." On that occasion the then leader of the opposition suggested that the word "advisory" should be added to the word "committees," and when the bill finally went through the house the words "advisory committees" were embodied in it. So that instead of one committee advising the minister, as we had under the legislation set up by the other government, we now have three committees advising. Well, if there is any change in policy in that respect, it is a change that gives the minister more advice than he had under the legislation of 1935.
Section 3, it is true, goes on to state how the committees shall be constituted, and as I pointed out last evening, the only difference between the committees as constituted now and the committee as constituted then, is that the farming population of the area concerned is represented by members appointed by the municipal bodies instead of by members appointed by the grain growers or other organizations of that type in that section of Canada.
Section 4 provides that the committee shall consider and advise the minister, and the section now reads:
The advisory committees shall consider and advise the minister as to the best methods to be adopted to secure the rehabilitation of the drought and soil drifting areas in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and to develop and promote within these areas systems of farm practice, tree culture, water supply-
In the legislation of 1937, in that section, just a few words were added:
. . . land utilization and land settlement. . . .
These activities were added to the others enumerated in the section; otherwise the legislation is exactly the same. The provision was broadened to the extent of adding the words " land utilization " in connection with the activities previously carried on, and the words " land settlement," which probably involve an enlargement of the activities under the bill.
Section 5 provided that no member of the committee should receive any pay, and that is still the condition. Section 6 provided:
The minister may appoint such temporary technical, professional and other officers and employees as he may deem necessary and expedient for carrying out the provisions of this act. . . .
That is exactly as it was. The minister does what he did in the legislation laid down by

Prairie Farm Rehabilitation
the previous government. Section 7 is identical with section 7 of the previous legislation:
The governor in council may make such regulations as may be necessary or expedient tor the effectual execution and working of this act and the attainment of the intention and objects thereof.
The only change in the next section is that instead of fixing a definite sum to be spent each year in connection with this legislation, the present legislation provides that we spend the sums given us through the estimates that pass this house from time to time.
I do not see any particular change in the policy of this government in relation to this matter, or in the principle of this legislation, from the principle which had been adopted in the previous legislation; and in so far as these sections which are added now are concerned, all the powers that are to be exercised under these three sections were previously exercised under section 7 of the original bill. These powers were all exercised by officials of the Department of Agriculture under the previous government. Their activities were continued by the present government, and, as I said the other day, many of the officials carrying on those activities in the department are the same officials that carried them on under the former government.
The statement with regard to these sections suggesting that the minister is given exceptional powers are hardly borne out by a careful reading of the legislation. Section 7 of the old bill provided that the governor in council might make regulations, and those regulations were the only provisions that really governed the activities of the minister. Under this particular legislation it is provided that the minister may, subject to section 4 of the act, that is subject to getting advice from the advisory committees, and with the approval of the governor in council, enter into agreements. We were entering into agreements before. We were doing all the things enumerated in this particular piece of legislation under the powers contained in section 7, and it is only because it is considered wise to ask this house to have those powers conferred directly by the house rather than have to depend upon order in council legislation in order to give the powers to the minister, that this particular bill has been brought in at this time.
There was one other remark made in regard to which I might say a word, that is the statement by the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Stevens) as to several thousands of undertakings; he went on to indicate that there are some 11,000 applications for undertakings in connection with which the sale of equipment would be involved. There is no government equipment used in the digging of dug-outs. These dug-outs are dug on the farms of farmers, usually with equipment provided by the farmer himself. When not constructed by farmers with their own equipment they are constructed with equipment that the farmers borrow from the municipality or some other body in the neighbourhood. Most of the other undertakings are not carried out with government equipment at all; they are carried out under contracts let by tender to contractors who use their own equipment. All the large dams are constructed in that way; all the large irrigation works are constructed in that way; all the ditch digging is done with equipment of that kind owned or controlled by contractors, and therefore not at the disposal of the government to sell.
Mr. PERLEY; Does the minister mean to say that all the dug-outs were dug with farmers' own equipment, that there was not government machinery going round, and after the farmers had taken off the surface did not government machinery come and finish the job?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND PERIOD OF OPERATION OF ACT, ETC.
speechtext:
No, the government
has no machinery going round doing that work. As regards work that is completed with what are known as drag-lines, these drag-lines belong either to municipalities or to contractors who have taken a contract from the farmers or through the municipality to clean out the bottom of the dug-out. In other words, what actually happened in Manitoba in connection with many of these undertakings is that the municipalities have made arrangements for drag-lines to be brought in to take out the bottom six feet of the dug-outs. So far as Saskatchewan is concerned in some instances groups of farmers formed into agricultural associations have secured drag-lines through contractors to come and do the same thing. This equipment does not belong to the government at all, and is not equipment over which the government would have any control either to sell or do anything else with. There are very few of the undertakings in any of the provinces in connection with which the government has control over any of the equipment. And much of that is carried on not under the set-up that is generally known as the P.F.R.A. set-up; it is carried on under the regular experimental farm set-up in those provinces. Take, for example, the leveling of lands in connection with irrigation undertakings; that is carried out under the direc-
Prairie Farm Rehabilitation

tion of the superintendent of the experimental farm at Swift Current, and the equipment purchased for the carrying out of the work is largely purchased under recommendation from those officials of the department, who are chosen not by the minister but by the civil service commission, regular officials of the Department of Agriculture carrying on the activities of the experimental farms branch.
I make those statements in order to clear up any suggestion that these thousands of undertakings are being carried on with government equipment and that this equipment is at the disposal of the minister to sell or do what he likes with. I suppose there would not be more than a dozen undertakings in Saskatchewan last year, probably not more than three or four in Alberta, and very few in Manitoba, on which equipment would be used with which the minister had anything whatever to do as to either purchase or sale.
In relation to the suggestion that under the previous government, a very careful check was kept of all the activities in connection with the department, exactly the same kind of check is being kept by the present government; more of it, because we are spending more money. And many of the same individuals, who were checking the accounts then are checking them now.
I say this in order to indicate that considerable care is being taken in connection with activities involving the expenditure of money in the department. It is only proper that these checks should be made of all expenditures of government money, whether in this department or in any other.

For example, the change suggested in section 3 largely has to do with the use of the word "guarantee" instead of "guaranteed analysis." Owing to the wide range of products coming under this act, the different uses of those products, and the fact that many of them do not lend themselves to chemical or other analysis, different lcinds of guarantee are required. Most of the products require a chemical guarantee; others require specific gravity and viscosity guarantee. There was reclassification which made permanent a number of temporary employees. I understand there is actually no increase.

Item agreed to.
J.'i. Branch farms, stations and illustration stations, $1,406,427.
Would the minister make a statement as to the work carried on at Indian Head experimental farm, with respect to rust resistant wheat?

There have been certain experiments carried on at the Indian Head farm for some time in connection with the growth of rust resistant wheats. The one which seems to have given the greatest satisfaction from the point of view of appearance, yield and in every other way, was grown in considerable acreage on the farm
this year. I visited the farm myself during the period when the rust was most prevalent in that section of the province, and that particular wheat had no traces of rust upon it whatsoever. Even Thatcher wheat growing in that community at that time did have rust on the leaves and on the stem below, what is known as black rust, which eats into the stem. But the particular wheat I speak of was entirely clear of rust, and it showed a very heavy yield when grown on land of the farm, running to forty and forty-one bushels to the acre. It is a very fine wheat, and an attempt is being made at the present time to put it out for multiplication so that it can be distributed throughout western Canada.
Is that designated as 975?
Yes, 975. It has recently been called Regent.

Is there going to be a
general distribution of small quantities of it to farmers?

There is a general
distribution being made now of about four bushels to different individuals who will grow iit this year, and that will multiply so that it can be distributed.
What steps does the farmer have to take to get the four bushels?
They make application to the Indian Head farm or the central experimental farm for it, and it is distributed as far as it will go to the individuals who apply.

May I be permitted under this item to ask the minister what progress is being made with experiments in regard to oats? I understand that some progress has been made in regard to Victory oats. It is of great interest to our eastern farmers.

There are two rust resistant varieties of oats, the Erbin, which is used in Ontario, and is being propagated I believe at Guelph, and the Vanguard oat, which is distributed in the western part of Canada, and in some parts of the east as well.
Would the minister indicate whether or not there is any distribution of these new oats among the farmers?

They are being propagated among the farmers. I purchased one hundred bushels of Vanguard myself this year from somewhere in Manitoba; I have forgotten the individual from whom I purchased it during the winter months. I think it can be obtained quite widely, and the Erbin oat can be obtained in the east.
2140	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
What is the present rate of wages paid to seasonal help on the Indian Head experimental farm?
The rate is twenty-seven cents an hour for seasonal labour, and from twenty-seven to thirty-three for year round labour.

There has been an
increase?
Yes, very materially.

Would the minister give details of the item, "Appropriation not required for 1939-40 "? In answer to a question which I asked of the minister on February 16, as reported at page 1044 of Hansard, concerning the "appropriation not required for 1939-40, $76,700," in connection with a previous vote, the minister replied:
The $76,700 is not taken out of this service. It was voted last year for buildings, and is not required this year because the buildings have been erected.
Upon investigation I find that buildings have nothing whatever to do with these particular votes, and I should like to have the break-down of this amount of $54,515, which is the appropriation not required for 1939-40, and is a credit.

I do not know where the hon. member made his inquiries, but I am informed by the officials who handle these matters that the $76,700 was the amount voted in our supplementary estimates last year for buildings, which have been constructed. This other item of $54,515 was also voted in the supplementaries last year for buildings, but the buildings are now built and we shall not require the money this year for that purpose.
Can the minister state to what extent Canus wheat has proved itself drought resistant?

I understand that nothing substantial has been done in that direction. Some attempts have been made to get a wheat that would stand drought better than other varieties, but I am quite sure that the hon. member for Acadia will understand that it is difficult to get anything to grow under drought conditions.

What progress has been
made with respect to the experimental farm at Smithers, British Columbia?

The land was secured, and I understand that a considerable part of it is cleared and that the house and barns are under construction. Some experimental work was carried on last year, but the farm is not yet in full operation.

I notice from the details given on page 57 of the estimates that a number of forestry engineers and forestry assistants are employed in connection with the branch farms and stations. What is the nature of the forestry work they carry on?

There are forestry farms at Indian Head and at Sutherland, which is just outside the city of Saskatoon. These forestry farms are conducted for the purpose of producing nursery stock, which is distributed to farmers throughout the prairie sections of western Canada.
Not any attempt at reforestation, but rather an attempt at beautification?

They are engaged in connection with that part of the prairie farm rehabilitation work which has to do with the planting of shelter belts and that kind of work.
Mr. COLDW'ELL: Will the minister give us some idea of what use is being made of this particular service at the present time? Is a greater use being made of it by the individual farmer? I know, of course, that a great deal of work has been done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and many trees planted in certain districts. In my own constituency, around Conquest, valuable work has been done which has been greatly appreciated. I am wondering just what effect the planting of shelter belts has had on the drought, and if any difference has been noticed.

Well, there is an open question, of course, as to the extent to which it assists in the matter of drought. I think there is grave doubt whether it has anything to do with producing more rainfall. Rainfall rather produces trees than the reverse. Valuable work is being done at Conquest under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act activities, also in the vicinity of Ivindersley, which is west of Conquest, and at other points. There has been a marked increase of recent yearn in the planting of trees, that is trees secured from these particular places. I am not in a position to state the extent to which that is on account of the fact that people are not so well off as they were a few years ago, and they may not be using more trees but they are getting more trees at the places they can get them at least cost, that is the farms operated by the department. I understand that nurseries in these sections have encouraged the giving out of trees from the forestry farm, because they think it induces the planting of more and more trees in those vicinities, and so they do more business at times when

Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
people can afford to purchase. But the trees that go out run into the millions. I am not in a position to give the number.

Would the minister comment on the possibility of overlapping between the federal farms and the provincial farms? I note that this is a vote for $626,000, and that it is S10.000 less than last year. Governments of all kinds are coming in for a great deal of criticism for over-taxation because of overgovernment.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I would point out to the hon. member that we are on item 14, not item 13.

I will ask my question on
another item.

The answer to the first part of the question, which does refer to item 14, is that there are no farms conducted by the provinces, excepting one in Ontario at Vineland, other than those which are associated with institutions, that is schools like the Guelph agricultural college and the farm which surrounds the Kentville school, which are operated in connection with the educational activities of the provinces. Only the provinces conduct activities having to do with education, and they have farms associated with those educational institutions.

How many of these
stations are there in Canada; how are they divided by provinces, and how many are there ini each province?

There is one in Prince Edward Island at Charlottetown; two in Nova Scotia, one at Kentville and one at Nappan; one in New Brunswick, at Fredericton; six in Quebec. Does the hon. member require the names?
What are those stations for?

They are experimental
farms and illustration stations. Referring to the fourteen branch farm stations and illustration stations, I may say there are three in Ontario; one at Ottawa, one at Harrow, and one at Kapuskasing; two in Manitoba; five in Saskatchewan-all put there, by the way, before I was minister-two in Alberta; four in British Columbia.

I notice that this is one of
the largest votes in the agricultural estimates. It mentions branch farms, stations, and illustration stations, and I believe that also there are some substations which have been set up under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. What is the difference between the operations in, say a branch farm, a station, an illustration station, and a substation?
There must be some system under which the operations of these different farms are carried out, indicating what their objective is.

The branch farms are
known as experimental farms. We have one central farm at Ottawa, and the others are known as branch farms. There are twenty-five of them. They are units which are doing some work that is supposed to be suited to the particular area in which they are located. Then there are what are known as stations, and they are rented sections of a man's farm. He is paid a certain rental for the land; he is allowed to grow certain crops, and he is allowed the proceeds of the crops. He carries on demonstration work under the direction of departmental officials for the benefit of those living in that community. They are illustration stations illustrating what has been learned on experimental farms elsewhere. The substations are of a little different type, usually rented as well. Some of them are owned by the government; but as a rule they are rented, the whole farm rather than just a part being rented, and operated for the carrying on of tests in connection with controlling soil drifting and work of that kind.
How many are there per province?

Stations and illustration
stations are mentioned. Is there any difference between the two? I understood from the minister that one is rented and one is not. There are a great number of illustration stations scattered throughout Canada, and some provinces seem to be especially favoured in regard to the number of illustration stations which they have. Could the minister tell us, while he is answering, what is necessary or in what way the illustration station is established? Does some particular community ask to have such a station in its particular vicinity, or how is the location of these stations determined, and when and where are they set up?

They may be asked for by people in the community or the department may select areas in which they think they should be. The branch farm is usually the parent farm in any particular province or area, and these stations are all included in the list which I read. Some of the farms in that list are what are known as experimental farms and the others are stations. The experimental farms are all owned and operated by the government. The illustration stations are farms which are rented from farmers and operated with the farmer himself having charge.
2142	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms

Just one more question. I notice that, for instance, a year ago there were in Saskatchewan fifty-one illustration stations; in Quebec there were also fifty-one; but in Ontario there were only seventeen. There might be one or two reasons for that. One, perhaps, is that the farmers of Ontario are a little better qualified to farm than are farmers in those other places; or it may be that they are not willing to ask for assistance or for these stations.

Maybe
they would not be granted,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are so shy.

Maybe they should ask for them. But I should like to know why it is that so many more stations have been set up in some provinces than in others. It seems to me that we all need education along those lines.

These are the illustration stations:
British Columbia	 18
Alberta	  11
Saskatchewan	 20
Manitoba	 12
Ontario	 17
Quebec	 52
New Brunswick	 18
Nova Scotia	 15
Prince Edward	Island	 13
One of the chief reasons for the differences as between Ontario and some of the other provinces is that there has not been the same demand for them in Ontario. Why that is I cannot say. I suppose some members may think Ontario farmers do not require the same amount of instruction. Whatever the reason is, there is not the same demand.
Are those the figures for 1937 or 1938?
Those are the latest figures.

The figures in the minister's report for the year ended March 31, 1938, are much different from those he has read. There was a difference of five or six in British Columbia, and there were differences all down the line. Are these illustration stations closed from time to time and new ones opened up?
Yes.
What is the reason for closing them?

After an illustration station has completed its work, it is closed. For example, a station is set up in some

area to demonstrate how a certain kind of land can be used. In a new section of Saskatchewan with which I am familiar, the growing of alfalfa seed has recently been developed. A few years ago there was no alfalfa seed growing there; the farmers did not think they could grow it. The natural thing is to establish an illustration station where it is found that the land is suitable for the purpose, and to indicate to the people what can be grown and in what manner. When that demonstration is completed and the people are conducting themselves as the department think they should, there is no further necessity and the expenditure is made somewhere else.

May I offer one suggestion? I do not find fault with these illustration stations; they do a great deal of good. The minister, however, might attempt one other thing by way of illustration. I suggest that somewhere in Ontario he set up an illustration station to demonstrate to the farmers how they can conduct their farms on a paying basis. If that were done, more good would be accomplished than by all the other illustrations that can be given the farmers. It is worth trying, because if we are to be taught this and that at stations, and by officials who are experts in their own line, they might be able to demonstrate to the farmers of Ontario and in different parts of the country how to conduct their farms so as to make them pay. It is a burning question in Canada to-day.

I believe the minister said there were eighteen stations in New Brunswick, fifteen in Nova Scotia and thirteen in Prince Edward Island. How many of these are devoting their energies along the line of fox farming?
Eight of them are fox farms.
In New Brunswick?
There are three in New Brunswick, three in Nova Scotia and two in Prince Edward Island.

The work that is being carried on in these particular stations is of a very high class and is having a beneficial effect on that particular industry. The man in charge of the experimental station just outside Summerside as well as the man in charge of the illustration station, I have reason to know, are doing wonderfully good work, and I should like on behalf of the industry to compliment the department upon having such splendid men as these in charge of that particular work. They have taken a real interest in it.

Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms

How many illustration
farms are operated with the farmer in charge?

All the illustration
stations.
In Saskatchewan?
Everywhere.
How many in Saskatchewan?

There are twenty illustration stations in Saskatchewan and thirty-one substations which are related to the prairie farm rehabilitation work. These are spread over the drought area. There are fifteen in Alberta and six in Manitoba.
As regards the substation at Regina, is the work carried on along the lines of experimenting with control of soil drifting?
Yes. The station at Regina is for the purpose of controlling soil drifting.
What is the result of the experiments at the Regina station?

They are carrying on two activities, one having to do with soil drifting and the other with weed control. Some of the work that has been developed in connection with soil control is to leave a sort of dressing of stubble and other material on the top, but it is generally recognized in the west that what holds the soil best, in the Regina district particularly, is rain, and if it does not rain, the soil blows in spite of everything one can do.

What
rental is given the farmers from whom these stations are acquired?

I think the best answer to that question is to read a summary of the contract that is entered into with those who operate:
1.	A rental of $5 an acre is paid where the plots do not exceed one-quarter acre each. Usually this plot area does not exceed one acre. On this class of work the supervisor puts in all the crop and harvests it.
2.	Where the plots are smaller than %o acre each, the operator receives $25 an acre compensation for the loss of the crop on such small areas.
3.	A rental of $3 an acre is paid where the blocks of land do not exceed three acres. The total area of such stations is frequently from twelve to fourteen acres. The operator handles all of this crop.
4.	A rental of $1 an acre is paid for the district experiment substations in the P.F.R.A. area in the prairie provinces. Large scale work is undertaken with strip farming, cover crops and surface tillage in connection with soil drifting control.
On some of these district experiment substations small plot experiments are also conducted.
5.	Special contracts have been made in connection with special work such as with cranberries, raspberries, hops and irrigation. None of these exceed $150 each. For certain operators along the line of the Hudson Bay railway an annual payment of $5 per acre is made while some of these operators receive no payment whatever.
For pasture experiments no rental is paid but the fertilizer is supplied free.
6.	Total maximum payments to any operator in eastern Canada is confined to less than $100.
In western Canada the limit is confined to below $200 for illustration station operators, while for operators of district experimental sub-stations the limit varies, being $1 an acre up to one section of land, plus payments for small experimental plots at the rates set for illustration station compensation. The upper limit, therefore, would not exceed $800 and usually is considerably less.

Who is
paid for putting the crop in; is it the farmer from whom the farm is rented? What is paid for the work done?
Nothing is paid to the farmer for his work. A rental is paid for the land on which the operation is carried on, but the farmer does all the work and gets the proceeds from the crop.
Is the farmer supplied with the seed?
Only where it is seed investigation work and where it is thought necessary to supply the seed because the test is of the seed.

Did I understand the
minister correctly to say that there are eleven illustration stations in Alberta?
I think that is correct, eleven of the one type and fifteen of the other.

Where are the eleven
stations located?
Iron Springs, Chedder-ville, Rocky Mountain House railway station Dickson. Leslieville, Stettler, Sangudo, Chau-vin, St. Paul, High Prairie, Fairview.

This particular item has grown by leaps and bounds since I have been in the house. Since the present minister has had control, there seems to be no thought of economy in the department. Look at this item 14, details of which are on page 57 of the estimates. I do not know where this standing army is going to end. And when one considers that the provinces have concurrent jurisdiction, why should the dominion establish a great big department like this?

2144	COMMONS
Supply-Agriculture-Experimental Farms
Look at some of these items-it puts me in mind of the army and navy added together -Chief supervisor of illustration stations, same as last year; senior agricultural scientist, forestry engineer, eleven experimental farm superintendents, all kinds of things; forestry engineer, animal nutritionist and genetecist, fourteen more experimental farm superintendents, five senior assistant agricultural scientists, two assistant superintendents, one assistant chief supervisor, another forestry engineer, an assistant agricultural scientist- there is no deputy assistant-two tobacco specialists, we have plenty of them in the lobbies all day long; an animal nutritionist and physiologist at $2,520, twenty-one more farm assistants of all kinds and grades, supervisors, irrigation specialist-they are all specialists-eighteen farm foremen amounting to $35,000 this year, $28,860 last year, an increase of $7,000, and no doubt more votes will be obtained this year. Then clerks, grade 4, forest assistants, a graduate assistant-one more graduate, no doubt of the agricultural college, eleven head herdsmen, nine of these at $1,800, one at only $1,785, a $15 deduction. Twelve head poultrymen, head gardeners, head beekeepers, head plotmen, head gardeners, grade 3, a stenographer, five poultrymen, a greenhouseman, more clerks, beekeepers, stenographers, herdsmen, gardeners, a part time assistant to dominion animal husbandman, one only caretaker, no janitors, and temporary assistance amounting to $117,000. Then, on the next page printing and stationery, rents, supplies and materials, et cetera, and travelling expenses, make a total of $1,406,427.
Where is the money to come from to pay all this? It has to come out of the income tax and the sales tax collected from the industrial provinces. Talk about economy! I commend this to the publisher of the Globe and Mail, the friend of my friend the minister, to find out what economy there is in this. Ballots might well be sent to all the farmers in this country to find out what they think of this department which has grown by leaps and bounds. These estimates should be dealt with on the municipal system, and we could sit - here and divide this million and a half dollars in half; let them get on this year with $750,000 to ran this branch of the army; that would be plenty for this department. With that kind of extravagance in this department, what is it going to amount to when they all -add it up and where is the money to come from? In view of these treaties I should think we would need fewer officials in the Department of Agriculture owing to the changes which have been made in the agreements to which I have referred.

It is eleven o'clock; I move that the committee rise and report progress.

It is still one minute to eleven. Before the hon. member takes his
seat-
I have not concluded my remarks.
-I should like to say that there are just the same number of employees in this branch of the department that there were last year.
I have not finished my remarks.
The hon. member moved a motion.
I have the floor. Both of us cannot talk at the same time.
There are just the same number as last year.

speechtext:
I should like to direct the following question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). In view of the vast amount of propaganda being

Privilege-Mr. Lacombe
carried on in Canada designed to undermine our democratic institutions and also to foster religious and racial hatreds, much of which emanates from abroad, will the government undertake a thorough public investigation into all forms of such propaganda?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION INTO ACTIVITIES INIMICAL TO CANADIAN INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman kindly sent me a copy of the question he intended to ask, and I wish to give this answer. There is no doubt that some propaganda along the lines suggested by the hon. gentleman is being carried out in certain parts of Canada. More particularly certain scurrilous and offensive publications are doing their utmost to undermine democratic institutions. One of their methods is to abuse parliament and slander public men. They have not been interfered with, mostly because of their insignificance and to avoid giving them a publicity which they relish. In some cases it would seem that they are the tools of foreign agencies interested in their destructive work. We are keeping a pretty careful watch over their activities, and we are prepared to protect Canadian laws and institutions, if needed.
I personally believe that a public investigation, whether by a parliamentary committee or a royal commission, might become desirable as to the existence, the activities and the financial support of all associations or societies which are carrying on subversive work, inimical to the institutions of Canada, and the suggestion of my hon. friend will be duly considered as to opportunity, time and form of such possible investigation.

Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of ways and means.
Mr. M.C. SENN (Haldimand): Mr. Speaker, I believe it is the time-honoured privilege which is accorded to representatives of the people to ask for redress of grievances and to bring before parliament matters of public importance when a motion of this kind is before the house or when the house is being asked to grant supply. I intend, therefore, to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the house a matter which I think is of paramount importance to Canadian agriculture.
Farming in Canada is a highly diversified occupation. Many different branches of agriculture are carried on in this country. The nature of the production on Canadian farms depends largely upon a number of factors, such as climate, types of soil, proximity to markets and to consumer centres of population.
According to the classification made by the Department of Agriculture and by the bureau of statistics we have the following branches of agriculture: wheat growing, field crops, dairying, live stock, fruits and vegetables, poultry products, and several others. The ones I have mentioned are of major importance, and all of them return a considerable amount of money to the farmer.
I should like to give the house an idea of the relative importance of these different branches of agriculture, as indicated by the following figures which I took the opportunity of getting from the bureau of statistics, showing the value of these different lines of farming in the nine years from 1930 to 1938 inclusive :
Value
Product	(in round figures)
Wheat	$1,557,000,000
Other field crops	 2,930,000,000
All farm animal products, including wool	 1,064,000,000
Dairy products	 1,805,000,000
Poultry and eggs	 482,000,000

I ask the house to note particularly the importance of the dairy industry and the live stock industry as indicated by the figures

I have just given. Dairying stands second and live stock fourth in order of importance.
The last census returns show that in Canada we have approximately 730,000 farms. More than half, probably two-thirds, of the farmers derive a considerable portion of their income from either dairying or live stock. Anything, therefore, which may have an adverse effect upon either of these two great branches of our agricultural industry should be carefully considered, and, if possible, measures should be taken to alleviate the situation.
In recent times increasing numbers of our cattle, sheep and hogs are being slaughtered and processed in the abattoirs of Canada. The price which the farmer receives for this live stock is determined, at least partly, by that which is received by the packers for the sale of the products and the by-products.
Animal fats in particular, in the form of edible and inedible lard and tallow, are one of these important by-products. It is estimated that each hog slaughtered in Canada will produce approximately fifteen pounds of lard. Each 1,000 pounds of cattle or sheep slaughtered will produce forty pounds of tallow. On this basis the average anual production of lard in this country is approximately 90,000,000 pounds and of tallow, some
100.000.	000 pounds. If we add to this the annual production of creamery butter, amounting to some 270,000,000 pounds, and the annual average production of dairy butter amounting to some 100.000,000 pounds, we have altogether a total of approximately
560.000.	000 pounds of edible animal fat produced in Canada annually.
The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), who, by the way, is my desk-mate, when speaking on this matter in the house in 1937, stated that the best authorities on dietetics placed the amount of fats required by human beings to maintain life in a climate like that of Canada at fifty pounds per person annually, which would mean that we require in this country each year 550,000.000 pounds of fat for human consumption. I believe that these estimates are well within the mark; they are quite conservative, so that the Canadian dairymen and live stock producers should be in a position to supply our human requirements or very nearly so.
In addition to these figures there is also a considerable amount of inedible fat produced in Canada-I refer to animal fats-which is also being displaced by the use of vegetable oils in the manufacture of soaps, grease and so on. In view of the figures I have just given, it seems to me that no one can fail to look with alarm upon the enormous annual increase in Canada's importation of vegetable﻿MARCH 22, 1939	2149

oils. This importation is accompanied, of course, by a corresponding, increase in the manufacture and sale of vegetable oil shortening in Canada and, as well, in the use of the inedible portion of these oils in the manufacture in Canada of certain products such as soap, lubricating greases and so on.
I should like now, if I may, to give the house a table of figures showing how these importations are increasing. It is true they are not listed as foods in the tariff item, but as a matter of fact they are refined and a very large proportion of them is used as food for human beings. The importations during the fiscal years I shall enumerate were:

These, in round figures, were the importations of vegetable oils in the years mentioned. I am sure the house will be struck with the rapid increase in these importations. These oils enter Canada in steamer loads at a very low price, absolutely free of duty, with the exception of a three per cent excise tax, and they are imported by a few firms whose processing costs are relatively inexpensive. After being refined, a large proportion becomes edible and enters into human consumption. I wish to give figures showing the tremendous increase in the production of vegetable oil shortening in Canada. The production in Canada, in the following years, was:
Year	Pounds
1932	 61,000,000

Since that time it has been impossible to obtain accurate figures showing the amount of vegetable oils produced in this country, owing to the refusal of the bureau of statistics to make public the figures of vegetable oils produced by two of the large competing companies in Canada. However, if we estimate the production last year according to the proportions of vegetable oils that were refined and used as human food in other years, it will easily amount to 145,000,000 or 150,000,000 pounds.
In addition to these vast amounts of vegetable oils which are rendered edible by processing and which are used for human food, there is a large proportion of the content of imported vegetable oils which is sold and used in the manufacture of certain commodities such as soap, and so on. It cannot be denied, I do not believe anyone will dispute the fact,
that because of the use of these imported oils there is a corresponding displacement of animal fats in the markets of Canada, and of butter, lard and tallow in use in our Canadian homes, and in manufacturing as well. Prices of butter in this country are to-day relatively low, and are in many instances below the cost of production. One cause of this is the fact that for a considerable length of time we have had more than a normal surplus of butter, ranging from 10,000,000 to 15,000,000 pounds above the average of other years.
Undoubtedly a considerable quantity of vegetable oils has been used instead of butter as shortening in the processes of cooking and baking, and I believe it is also true that evidence is not lacking that a certain quantity of vegetable shortening is used as spread in place of butter. It is difficult, of course, to estimate to what extent this is carried on, but I venture to say-I do not think there is any doubt about it-that of the 150,000,000 pounds of vegetable shortening produced and sold in Canada last year, sufficient was used in place of butter to account for the abnormal surplus of butter we have on hand at the present time.
In addition to the replacement of Canadian butter by the use of vegetable oil shortening, there is a corresponding or even a greater displacement of lard and tallow which are rendered from the fat of hogs, sheep and cattle. In restaurants and bake-shops, and in many private houses particularly, because of the intensive campaign of advertising which has been carried on by those companies that are refining vegetable oils and placing them on the market, these are being used rather than Canadian products.
I can recall distinctly the agitation and the debates that took place in this house between 1922 and 1924 regarding the manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. There was at that time a keen division of opinion respecting the matter. It was necessary for a bill to be introduced each year to authorize the continued manufacture and importation of oleomargarine. It was not until 1924 that no further bill was introduced ' and oleomargarine no longer allowed to be produced in or imported into Canada. I think it is within the memory of many hon. members that between 1925 and 1930 there was a constant annual increase in the importation of New Zealand butter. This increase continued until the dairy industry of this country became so alarmed, and there was such an insistent demand to revoke the order in council which allowed New Zealand butter to come in under a duty of one cent a pound, that it was finally revoked, I believe, when

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the budget was brought down in 1930 by my lion, friend who is now Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). If importations of these small amounts of oleomargarine and New Zealand butter had the effect of injuring the dairy and live stock industries of Canada, as evidently the farmers of Canada believed they did, how can we sit quietly by at this time and watch the large importations of vegetable oils entering this country and replacing our Canadian produced animal fats, without taking any action whatever?
Fluctuations in the price of by-products manufactured from slaughtered cattle, hogs and sheep, have, as I have already stated, a direct effect upon prices paid to the producer for those animals on the hoof. Prices quoted in the live stock markets and the stockyards are based on the returns received from every part of the animal when processed; the better the market for the by-products, the more the farmer should get for the live animal.
Mr. Stanley McLean, president of Canada Packers, Limited, delivered an address before the Holstein Breeders' Association at the Royal York hotel in Toronto in 1936. He is reported in the Globe and Mail of that date to have stated that the granting of an application, made by certain interested parties, which was then before the tariff board, would probably increase the price to the farmer one-fifth of a cent a pound on cattle and one-third of a cent a pound on hogs. Subsequently a statement was made to the tariff board by those who made the application; they also stated that if their request were granted, the additional return to the farmer would be about SI a head on every hog and at least $2 a head on every finished cattle beast sold. A conservative estimate based on these figures would indicate that Canadian farmers are losing about $6,000,000 annually in the price which they receive for their cattle and hogs owing to the increase in the use of vegetable oils and fats and shortenings in this country.
For a number of years we had a good market for Canadian lard in the British isles. We were able to export our lard at attractive prices; because of that the price of lard remained at a fairly good level until a year or two ago, when prices dropped in the British market, and we have now lost that market entirely, or nearly so. In 1936, another thing happened which had a detrimental effect upon the lard producers of this country. The government of the United States passed the Bailey amendment imposing on all fats entering that country an excise tax of three cents a pound over and above the regular rates which were in effect at that time. As
fMr. Senn.]
a result of this action our market in the United States fqr our surplus fats has been practically lost, and prices of animal fats in Canada have accordingly dropped to most unprofitable levels. This excise tax was of course also applied to vegetable oils imported into the United States. In certain instances an additional processing tax of three cents a pound, and 4i cents a pound on another group of vegetable fats entering the United States, was imposed. These taxes had the immediate effect of decreasing by about twenty per cent the amount of vegetable oils entering the United States. The effect of this was immediately felt by producers of animal fats of different kinds over there. It also resulted in a reduction of from 30,000,000 to 40,000,000 pounds in Canadian fats entering the United States, which had a very serious effect upon prices of lard and tallow in Canada.
Early in 1926 an application was made to the tariff board by a group of packing house companies not interested in the importation and processing of vegetable oils, together with the national dairy council and manufacturers of inedible animal greases, fats and oils. They applied for revision of the customs tariff on all fats and greases entering Canada except butter and cream. The hearing of this application took place on December 9, 10 and 11, 1936, over two years ago. Yet, as far as I am able to learn, no finding has been brought down. I believe the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) asked a question of the Minister of Finance yesterday, and if I understood the minister's reply correctly, no finding has yet been brought down. I cannot imagine that the tariff board has not reached a decision on this matter in two years. It is difficult to know why its finding has not been submitted to the finance minister, unless it be that perhaps he is not anxious to have it.
