speechtext:
This question was dealt with on the floor of the house in 1936 by my colleague who sits to my right (Mr. Harris), and it has been discussed every year since in this house, so that the finance minister and

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the government cannot plead ignorance of it. They must be alive to the situation and what is going on.
The action taken by the government of the United States is in direct contrast with that of the government here. I have already told the house of the measures taken by the administration of that country to protect the interests of farmers producing animal fats in the United States. I am making this statement at this time in the hope that something may be done in the near future for farmers producing this line of goods in Canada.
It is true that there are in this country certain interests who are opposed to any action being taken. But I point out that the action which was taken by the United States government in imposing excise tax and processing tax upon the importation of vegetable oils into that country did not increase the price over there of the different brands of vegetable oil shortenings produced in that country. As a matter of fact, although these oils enter Canada entirely free of duty and with no excise tax, prices in Canada and the United States to-day for vegetable oil shortenings are practically on a par. I had a report a few days ago which quoted vegetable oil shortening in tierces in Chicago at nine cents a pound, and in Toronto at eight cents a pound. But adding the sales tax of eight per cent to the Canadian price makes them practically equal.
No matter how important foreign markets may be, the fact remains that the home market is the farmer's most valuable asset. He has to buy in a protected market. I believe that the Canadian market should as far as possible be preserved for goods manufactured in Canada. But I am equally convinced that Canadian farmers also should as far as possible enjoy the full benefit of the home market. They should not be placed in the position of having their products pushed off the home market and undersold by cheap substitutes imported free of duty from countries with low standards of living and low production costs.
Our friends on the government benches, I know, always shy away at the word "protection." They seem to have an obsession against tariffs, or at least the government seem to be afraid to impose customs duties for fear of offending some of their supporters. It is true, of course, that they leave in effect customs duties already imposed; but why should we attempt to protect the Canadian dairyman, for example, by placing and leaving in effect a duty of five cents a pound on butter, while at the same time we allow vegetable oils to come into this country absolutely free of duty in order to take the place of that butter?
Why should a tariff be imposed on the importation of lard in order to protect producers of lard in this country, while at the same time we allow vegetable oils to come in absolutely free?
Yesterday we heard an hon. member on the government side compliment the Minister of Finance upon a small reduction, amounting to some 124 per cent, in the duty on cream separators. On a separator costing $100 this would mean about $12, if the purchaser got the full benefit of the reduction. The life of a cream separator is at least ten or twelve years, which would mean that the dairyman who bought that separator would benefit to the extent of possibly $1 a year. At the same time we allow these vegetable oils to come into this country to replace butter and all kinds of animal fats. Up to the present nothing has been done about the matter, although the government has known of the situation ever since it has been in office.
I know it is useless to ask the government to impose duties for the protection of the dairymen and live stock producers of Canada, but in conclusion I should like to suggest that they might at least follow the course that has been pursued by the government of the United States and impose some processing tax or excise duty. I warn the government that the situation is bad; it is growing worse and becoming more critical as the days go by.

Mr. Speaker, the subject under discussion is one which deeply affects the business in which I am interested, that is, agriculture. I believe it is highly important that the government should give careful consideration to the remarks of the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and the sound logic of his arguments; and because of the urgency of the situation I cannot resist the temptation to express my approval of what has been said by the hon. member.
There are two features I should like to discuss, without unduly trespassing on the time of the house and without repeating what has been said so well by the hon. member, in reference to the increasing importations of vegetable oils into this country. In the first place it is vitally important that we protect the health and sustenance of our own people. In the second place we should seek to bring about national prosperity by maintaining agricultural stability. Nature has provided vegetable oils for use as foodstuffs in tropical zones, but in the cold and rigorous climate of this country it has long been recognized that animal fats provide better food for our people. So I think we should discourage the growing

2152	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
tendency to depend upon foreign producers of foodstuffs. If we engaged in a world war it might be very difficult to bring to this country fifty steamers, each carrying the equivalent of a trainload of vegetable oils, which we would have to do in order to maintain the importations of the last few years. Since a very large percentage of these huge shipments has been made up of edible oils, I believe this is a factor that must be seriously considered at this time.
We have seen this dangerous competition to Canadian producers growing in this dominion for many years. As the hon. member for Haldimand has said, I recall that a few years ago, when four or five million pounds of oleomargarine were being consumed in this country, many members of this house rose almost in rebellion against the importation or manufacture of this commodity. As a result the government of the day, which I believe was supported by the party sitting opposite, prohibited further importations of oleomargarine by means of increasing the tariff. To-day we find 255,000,000 pounds of vegetable oils flooding our markets, and our people becoming more and more dependent upon this type of foodstuff.
I mention that as a matter of vital importance to the consuming public of this country. I believe it is highly important that we should maintain a sound agriculture in Canada, and in my opinion the stability of this great industry can be best brought about by developing greater diversity of production. I think this would have a direct effect on the greatest problem facing Canada to-day, namely that of the employment of our people. Last year I suggested that the government, through the economics branch of the tariff board, carry on a methodical research in order to ascertain the effect of these huge importations of vegetable oils on the live stock industry of Canada. So far as I know no such research has been undertaken, in spite of the fact that our importations last year showed an increase over the year 1936 of approximately 60,000,000 pounds.
The importance of this issue has been emphasized by the hon. member for Haldimand, but I should like to remind the house once more that there are 750,000 families on farms throughout Canada, and in addition an enormous number of hired men employed on these farms. Over 500,000 of these farmers are breeders of live stock, with over $4,000,000,000 invested in lands and buildings; and it must be remembered that climatic conditions in Canada force thosh engaged in the production of animal fats and dairy products to house their live stock with some care and (Mr. W. E. Rowe.]
at considerable expense. We have 500 million dollars invested in live stock, over 600 million dollars invested in equipment, and the agricultural industry pays 100 million dollars annually to the wage earners of this country. It pays $54,000,000 in property taxes. I mention only these few features to remind hon. members that the farming industry has always been regarded as the backbone of Canada. Many hon. members have been in this house much longer than I, but they will remember that at least ten years ago I urged upon the government the dangers of a lopsided development of our Canadian agricultural industry. Since that time I have watched a continuous lopsided development. Yesterday we amended the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, a piece of legislation which will cost this country two or three million dollars. Last year we paid $60,000,000 as a wheat bonus to relieve this lopsided development. What has this government done? In fact they did nothing from 1921 to 1930 by way of a study of this all important problem. This government's policy has shown a tendency to develop in such a way as to threaten the very lifeblood of Canadian agriculture. I have stated in this house that the time would come when we would regret this lopsided development, when we would regret not having encouraged a greater diversification of production in this industry. I well recall what one of my friends from western Canada said to me at that time. He was a delightful gentleman who sat down here to my left, but even he was defeated at the subsequent election. He said that we did not understand wheat production, that western Canada would always be the bread-basket of the world. He felt that they were almost guaranteed dollar wheat for many years to come. Only one year afterward, every elevator in this dominion was loaded up with unsold wheat.
I have heard the idea advanced on scores of occasions that we must buy where we can buy the cheapest, that only in such countries could we hope to sell the wheat produced on the vast prairies of western Canada. Since I have been a member of this house I have seen one after the other of those countries raise their tariffs. I shall not take the time to refer to them individually, but every member within the sound of my voice will recall that those countries raised their tariffs, in many cases to a point where the duty imposed was more than the price of Canadian wheat. We might as well face the facts. Through a haphazard agricultural policy we have risked the future prosperity of Canada. We have placed ourselves at the mercy of the whims of foreign countries. We must face the chances of weather conditions throughout the

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
world and compete with chemical substitutes which have been developed to take the place of flour made from No. 1 northern wheat, which we were told so often was impossible of substitution.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WITH RELATION TO DAIRYING, LIVE STOCK AND VEGETABLE OILS
speechtext:
Before we worry about the markets of Ontario for pork products, I suggest that we first fill the quotas provided by the empire trade agreement of 1932. I suggest some of this production would be consumed by the additional hired help that would be necessary to carry on the development of mixed farming activities. Although my farm is slightly larger at the present time, on many occasions I have kept four heads of families employed on 100 acres. As compared with that, it is possible for an ablebodied man to farm 600 acres planted in wheat alone with the type of machinery that has been developed in recent years. No other avenue of endeavour in this dominion offers more possibilities for the establishment, not only of remunerative employment, but also of happy homes. I am referring to employment because the hon. member has brought it up.
All I ask the hon. member to do is to look across the border at the state of Minnesota. Within the lifetime of the youngest member of this house, that state produced more wheat than Alberta and	Manitoba	combined.
Thirty-five or forty years ago no doubt the prairie farmers of Minnesota felt that state would be a great wheat producing district for many long years to come. But a gradual diversification of production was brought about as a result of climatic conditions, loss of fertility of the soil, and other
71492-136i
causes. Minnesota produces only a small amount of wheat compared with what she produced some years ago, but she now produces more dairy products than the whole of the Dominion of Canada. This is the type of diversified and intensive agriculture which has kept the farms of Europe fertile for a thousand years. As I have said, we cannot keep on forever robbing the soil of its fertility. You cannot wisely continue to encourage only one product and depend solely upon an export market for its disposition, and depend upon the whims of every government of the world.
We are considering a plan under which the treasury of Canada is to provide $50,000,000 or $60,000,000 for one section of the dominion in order to encourage the production of an article which the world seems to desire less to-day than it did a few years ago. I suggest to the government of the day that they stop, look and listen; that they notice the signs of the times. In other words, they should come up to date and encourage the type of industry which will not only provide more employment but bring about more stability in national income and exports. There is an old agricultural saying that one should not put all his eggs in one basket. That adage was never more sound than it is to-day, so far as Canadian agriculture is concerned.
To my mind the basic stability of Canadian agriculture depends upon the effects and influences of three distinctive things. It depends, first, on markets for our products; second, on productive efficiency, and third, on soil fertility. If anyone can show me that the trend of the agricultural policy of this government has assisted in any one of these phases, I will say that this government might have a chance to return to power. But nothing has been done in that direction since 1935. In fact nothing was done by the same party between 1921 and 1930 to develop Canadian agriculture on a sound and stable basis.

a man against his will and he is of the same opinion still; I shall not pursue that any further with the Minister of Finance. But I suggest to him that before bringing down the budget of this year he consider carefully having reports from the tariff board, and consider also the advisability of giving to the farmers of this dominion similar protection to that which our industrialists enjoy. I say further to him that if he does not do that, he will not write the next budget that is brought down in this house.
For many years we had greater exports to markets overseas for our live stock products than we have now. My hon. friend shakes his head. May I remind him that we sold more live stock products in the British market in 1921 than we have sold in any year since. We sold more cheese 30 years ago by far than has been sold since, and we sold more live stock products by millions of dollars in 1921 than this country sold of wheat in that year. We have had a government now for some years with a wheat complex. May I remind the minister that the greatest market for all our Canadian agricultural produce is the home market; for every dollar the home consumer spends for Canadian wheat he spends eight dollars for live stock and dairy products. The ratio is 8 to 1. We consume in our home market from 80 to 85 per cent of our agricultural products. Contrast that with our sister dominions, Australia and New Zealand. They export about 85 per cent of their agricultural products and consume 15 per cent, while we consmue about 95 per cent and more of our live stock and dairy products and other products of intensified agriculture. The large consuming markets for our live stock products and the products of our intensified agriculture, such as poultry, fruits and vegetables, are along the seaboard, in Montreal and other large centres like Toronto.
May I remind my western friends that it costs a great deal to bring their products from the west to the east. It costs $3.33 a hundredweight to bring their butter east, while vegetable oils from overseas competing with our Canadian animal products arrive at the port of Montreal by paying 25 cents a hundred.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WITH RELATION TO DAIRYING, LIVE STOCK AND VEGETABLE OILS
speechtext: Is there not a surplus of butter in Ontario right now?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WITH RELATION TO DAIRYING, LIVE STOCK AND VEGETABLE OILS
speechtext:
Yes, we have a surplus of dairy butter. We had at the beginning of the year about 44 million pounds, and we are importing 255 million pounds of vegetable oils-167 million pounds approximately of the edible type. There has been a reduction of seventy per cent in the consumption of dairy butter for bakery purposes during the last eight years. I submit that the 44 million pounds of butter that await a market to-day might well be consumed in this country if we consumed it at the same rate as that at which we are using imported vegetable oils.
I mentioned a tariff on vegetable oils. 1 realize that it might be difficult to place a tariff on vegetable oils; I would suggest rather the imposition of a processing tax that would equalize the conditions between our farmers and those who produce under more favourable conditions. It is so easy in tropical zones to produce vegetable oils very cheaply, and it is unfair for any government, whether Liberal or Conservative, to maintain high tariffs for the protection of our soap makers, cake makers, biscuit manufacturers and other processors and refuse similar treatment to our farmers. Our farmers have very high expenses compared with those of farmers in tropical countries, where people scarcely need to wear clothes, let alone to house their cattle. This government should be alarmed at the increase in the importations of vegetable oils. When you stop to think that we import more vegetable oils than, we produce of dairy butter, surely it is time for the government to take cognizance of the situation. I know that farmers even on the other side of the line view with amazement the inaction of the Canadian government on this issue, and I can quite understand as I read from "American Farmer" their saying "before we try to help the Canadian farmers by the United States agreement we have made with that country, they ought to be protecting their own market."
We have in Canada great possibilities, but the inaction of the government makes one doubt whether under its policies agriculture can be maintained as our great basic industry. We live in a cold climate, and in live stock production the cost of bams in old Ontario, and in some parts of western Canada, is almost as much as the farms are worth to house the stock.
I think we must consider carefully the maintenance of our home market. All who are within sound of my voice will agree that our huge importations are seriously affecting

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
the live stock industry of this country, and threatening to affect it very seriously in the years to come.
Another means of encouraging stability in agriculture in this country is through productive efficiency. By that I mean, not the individual efficiency of the farmer but the efficiency of our country, our national efficiency. This government should lose no time in making a careful survey of agricultural conditions. Nobody knows what their policy is; in fact, they scarcely know from one day to the next what it is going to be. One day it is a bonus on something of which we now have too much; another day it is a bonus for acreage on which less is going to be produced; all this, in an endeavour to get away from that vicious word " protection." Yet they grant subsidies up to $60,000,000- which I submit is a more vicious policy than the protection applied to any industry in Canada. At the same time they remove the excise tax on products coming into this country, although they need revenue very badly. I am amazed that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) has stood for that. On his right he has the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), paying $60,000,000 for the production of something which we cannot now sell. On his -left he has the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin), waiting to spend $100,000,000 for election purposes, and on his own desk he can read where he is going to have what will probably be a huge deficit. He will surrender twelve to eighteen million dollars of revenue by the removal of the excise tax, and at the same time watch the Minister of Public Works throw twelve million dollars into a sink-hole in Montreal for a terminal which is not required.
I am satisfied that when we have national planning based on a national survey, agricultural development will follow. We have watched the progress of the United States during the last few years.
I believe that in 1933 we imported a small quantity of palm oil, about 287,000 pounds. But after it was found that it could be made more edible, imports increased until in 1938 we brought in over 70,000,000 pounds of that product. The hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has pointed out what has been its practical effect on the live stock producers of this country. Mr. J. S. McLean, of Canada Packers, Limited, has stated that it did not mean very much to those of us who are engaged in farming. He said it represented only twenty cents per hundredweight on cattle and thirty-three cents per hundredweight on hogs. Well, on our present production that would mean $8,800,000 a year. I submit that
even those who are engaged in other enterprises will agree that an additional income of nearly $9,000,000 would stimulate production in other lines of business. There are many farmers throughout our districts who would spend a little more if they had a little more to spend. I know of many farmers' wives who could do with a new suit this spring; many of whom have not bought one since this government came into power. I know many of our people who would buy new equipment if they could get a share of that $9,000,000. It would certainly mean something to the general business activity of this country. [DOT]

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WITH RELATION TO DAIRYING, LIVE STOCK AND VEGETABLE OILS
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the addresses by the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe). They have made a fine presentation of a serious situation that confronts the dairymen of Canada at the present time. For several sessions I have called the attention of parliament to the great handicap that the dairymen and live stock men in Canada are labouring under by reason of a product made from vegetable oils imported from tropical countries, and also owing to the reduction in the tariff on butter. These two factors have contributed to the present depressed price of butter. Last year, 1938, we brought into Canada 5,500,000 pounds of butter. That came into a country which is producing more butter than it can consume. On January 1, 1939, we had almost 44,000.000 pounds of butter in cold storage, or 16,000,000 pounds more than the quantity in storage on January 1, 1938.
In Canada we manufacture some of the finest cheese sold on the British market, but our butter has not been looked upon very favourably there; in fact, it takes only fourth or fifth place. It is highly important that the fanners and dairymen of Canada should export their surplus milk in the form of cheese, and never attempt to make butter for export. Briefly, the reason is that we are competing with a country where the cattle graze outdoors the year round, where large herds are kept, where they can support a cow on every acre, not like the farms that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was
2158	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
telling us about last night where it takes fifty acres to graze one animal. They milk twice a day and send * the milk to large factories where it is made scientifically and uniformly into butter, grass butter, the year round; whereas in Canada we have to stable our cattle for six or seven months of the year and provide fodder for them. Here also we have only small factories, and the practice is to collect the cream two or three times a week. The cream comes into the factory in all states of acidity, so that it is difficult to make butter from it to compete with that of New Zealand. The butter we make in Canada is very good if it is used within a few weeks after it is made, but put it in cold storage for three months and it is rancid. New Zealand butter stored for three months is as sweet as the day it was made. Therefore it is impossible for us to compete with that country in butter.
The value of the dairy products made in Canada in the past ten years exceeded by many thousands of dollars the entire value of our wheat production; yet in this house we hear nothing but wheat, wheat. We vote millions of dollars every year to buy seed wheat; we peg the price for wheat, and last night we heard in this house of a scheme- which is no new scheme; it has been going on for some time-to irrigate land where it requires fifty acres to graze one animal, in order to try to grow wheat on it, a product that is already a drug on the market. Why are we bolstering up wheat all the time? Moreover, wheat is grown to any great extent, in only three provinces, namely, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, while dairy farming is practised in every province. Dairying is far more important than wheat growing. The weekly cream cheque that came to farmers in the western provinces during the years when their crops were short kept hundreds of them off relief. Yet these very farmers, with scarcely any other income, were competing with butter made in a country like New Zealand, and shortenings made from vegetable oils imported from tropical countries.
The consumption of wheat in Canada is not very large. If we take the last three years, the average was four bushels per capita. If we take the average price for three years, this means that we spent annually $32,000,000 on wheat. But the amount spent annually in the past three years for meat and dairy products was $275,000,000. The per capita consumption of farm products annually for the past three years was sixty-four pounds of beef, sixty-five pounds of pork, six pounds of mutton, thirty-one pounds of butter, three and a half pounds of cheese and four bushels

of wheat. Of milk and dairy products we consume 647 pounds per capita a year.
We have in Canada 750,000 farmers, the great majority of whom are either dairymen or producers of live stock. These farmers ask to be given the same measure of protection that is given to the dairymen in the republic to the south of us. Canada to-day can produce all the butter and all the animal fats' that we can consume in this country. A few years ago this government in their wisdom prohibited the manufacture and sale of oleomargarine in Canada. That was a great boon to the dairy farmers; it was a good law. But to-day we are faced with a far greater menace than oleomargarine ever was, a . product made from these cheap vegetable oils imported free into Canada from tropical countries. In 1933 the entire importation of vegetable oils of all classes was 91,000,000 pounds. By 1938 that had increased to 255,000,000 pounds.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) stated a moment ago that the late government had taken no action in this matter. I point out to him that this menace had not in those years reached the proportions that it has to-day. In 1933, 67,000,000 pounds of shortening manufactured from vegetable oils were sold in Canada. But by 1938 that had increased to 120,000,000 pounds. And just as the sale of shortenings made from vegetable oils increased, so the sale of shortenings made from animal fats decreased.
These oils come from tropical countries, and are marked " not for food." But after they come into this country they are processed by a few of our large combines that are making immense wealth out of the sale of this product. The better part of the oil is manufactured into shortening and put on the shelves of every grocery store in the country, coming in direct competition with our butter and lard. The residue is sent to our soap factories, where it again comes in competition with animal fats from our abattoirs. In 1936 the government of the United States placed against these vegetable oils duties which totaled about six cents a pound on oils other than crude, 4i cents a pound on crude oils and 3i cents a pound on tallow. Before that duty was imposed, we had a market for tallow in Chicago, but ever since that time our tallow has sold in Toronto for just 3i cents less than the Chicago price. In 1935 the price of tallow in both Toronto and Chicago was nine cents a pound; there was no duty, and the price just leveled up. Since then, however, it has been unprofitable to ship our fats to the United States.
We do not want to prohibit entirely the
importation of vegetable oils. That is not the

Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
idea. We do want a tariff or restriction or processing tax placed upon it, so that prices of butter and lard may not be unduly depressed. I realize that a great deal of the oil brought in is used for medicinal purposes, for canning fish and in certain lines of manufacture. With this we have no quarrel. I am a protectionist; I believe in the principle of protection, because in the world to-day, when every country is protecting its own interests, it is foolish to talk about anything else. It is a question of regulating that protection so that it will not unjustly benefit or unjustly harm any individual or any part of the country. I am in favour of protection for the farmer. 1 believe the farmers are just as much entitled to protection as are our industrialists, and further I say that agriculture and industry are not enemies. They are partners in this country, and they must work together. When you create employment you create markets for agricultural products. If the men and women engaged in industry have steady employment at good wages they do not care whether they pay twenty or thirty cents a pound for butter; but to-day, with our people out of work or working only two or three days a week, butter is extremely dear at twenty cents a pound. Give our people employment; keep our industries going and you will create markets for our agriculturists. Not long ago I noticed a statement by the manager of one of our large packing houses, an organization engaged in the importation of this oil and making immense profits out of it, a gentleman who knew whereof he spoke. He said he was confident that the sale of shortening and soaps produced from vegetable oils reduced the price of every hog in Canada by $1, of every steer by $2, and of the production of every dairy cow by $2. When that was figured up, it came to something between S8,000,000 and $10,000,000 that the farmers of this country were losing in this way.
It takes a farmer six months to raise a 200 pound hog. In the first place there must be careful breeding and in the second place careful feeding to produce a 200 pound hog in that time. It can be done and is done, but the man who does it must know his business. That hog will produce only fifteen pounds of lard. It takes three years to produce a steer weighing 1,100 pounds, which will produce fifty pounds of edible tallow. But out of 100 pounds of palm olive kernels, forty-five pounds of oil can be produced at very little cost. Let us be sensible about these matters. There is no use in talking free trade, protection or anything else. Let us talk business. Is it fair that these people should be permitted to come to this cold country, where we require so
much food, so much fuel and so much clothing, and where we are proud of the fact that the standard of living is so high, and to compete with us on these terms? In the United States they have protected their farmers, and those who read journals coming from that country [DOT] will be aware that an agitation is being carried on by the organized farmers to have the protection increased against the importation of vegetable oils.
A moment ago the Minister of Finance said the whole matter of vegetable oils had been referred to the tariff board and that the government was awaiting the decision of that board. To my knowledge this question of vegetable oils was referred to the tariff board on December 10, 1936, and now we are at the end of March, 1939. If it takes the tariff board two years and four months to reach a decision on an important matter of this kind, while the farmers are labouring under such a disadvantage, there must be something wrong with the tariff board. Surely we should have a report in less than that length of time.
This is a matter of vital importance. I am not trying to make political capital out of it; I am speaking in the interests of the farming community to wrhich I belong, and to which my family have belonged for four generations. I am speaking on a question that I understand. I know the requirements of the farmers of this country; I have been engaged in farming and have been connected with farmers' organizations practically all my life. This question is above politics; it is above partyism. It is a matter we are bringing up in justice to our agriculturists, in order that those~engaged in dairying may be placed upon a safe foundation.
I was going to mention another matter on which I have a note here; but it might be thought I was trying to make some political capital out of it, so I will leave it out. It had to do with the duty imposed on our cattle going into the United States. We pay practically $15 a head under the quota, and when we have used up our quota we pay $30 a head. I am referring to the average steer weighing 1.000 pounds. Then we permit the free importation of 30,000 head of cattle from the United States and the Argentine in tin cans. That is what the farmer of to-day has to consider. If we are going to live in a country where protection is necessary, our agriculturists should get their fair share of that protection.
While the importation of butter into this country and the sales of shortening have depressed the price of butter to a considerable degree, there is something else which is of
2160	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
vital interest. I refer to the under-consumption of butter through so many of our people being on relief or perhaps working only one or two days a week. These people are not able to consume the butter they would consume if they had steady employment at good wages. That factor enters into the problem.
The one thing we need more than anything else in this country is confidence. Our people seem to be afraid. Capital is running to cover. People are putting their money into government bonds which pay two or three per cent, or they let it lie in the banks at per cent. What are they afraid of? Most of them will say they are afraid of taxation. They do not want to invest in land or in the building of a home. To-day the price of agricultural land is fifty per cent of what it was ten or twelve years ago. You cannot build a home in any town or city in Canada and sell it for what it costs you to build. You cannot rent ;t and make a profit after paying taxes. There is sufficient money lying in our banks to build all the homes required, provided they could be built at a profit. The government would not need to go into the building business.
I have nothing further to say, except that I plead with the government. The Minister of Finance has left his seat; but the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who I know is just as deeply interested in this question as I am, is here, and I trust he will use his influence to see that the great farming class to which he belongs gets a square deal so *far as the dairy industry is concerned.

I took the years 1935 and 1937. Notwithstanding all that has been said about the difficulties of the farmers, I was very happy to hear the hon. member for Dufferin- . Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) say that a solution of the great problem was a back-to-the-land movement. I heartily endorse that suggestion.
I believe that if sixty per cent of the people were on the land and forty per cent were in the cities, we would not have the present problem to the same extent. But owing to the system under which we operate, there has been a magnetic influence drawing boys from the farm, and it is not the boys who have come from the farms that go to the offices for relief they all have jobs. They have displaced, however, many who ordinarily would have the work they are doing.
In spite of the unfortunate condition of affairs among our farmers, as depicted to us, and the fact that they are not receiving a large enough share of the national income,
I would point out that seventy-five per cent of the people on the farms own their own homes, whereas in a larger city there is a smaller percentage of home owners. In cities of 30,000 and over, only forty-five per cent of the people own their own homes; in towns of 5,000, fifty-eight per cent; and in towns of

Canada-United. States Trade Agreement
less than 1,000, seventy-one per cent; while, as I say, seventy-five per cent of the people in the rural districts are home owners.
The hon. member for Haldimand and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe waxed eloquent in advocating that something be done by this government for the farmers. May I point out for their information that in 1934 the total number of commercial failures in Canada was 1,690 as compared with 952 in 1937. I point out some of these facts because I know that industry cannot prosper unless our farmers are prosperous; and I have no doubt that the condition of the farmers would have been a great deal worse had there not been a change of government in 1935.
Reference has been made to the competition of our farmers with New Zealand in regard to butter. If you take the record of importations of New Zealand butter you will find that, as the hon. member for Sherbrooke pointed out, at the time we were importing butter, the price was far in excess of the ability of the average person to pay. I do not think that hon. members will agree with me, but I believe that if the price had not been allowed to reach the high figure that it did, which had the effect of stimulating butter production, with the result that more milk went into the production of butter owing to that excessive price, we would not have had the trouble we have to-day. Unfortunately a great deal of milk which should have gone into the production of cheese went into the production of butter. That was brought about by the high price of butter. The only regret I have is that the lady friends of the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) did not get out on the streets a month or two earlier and boycott butter before the price got so high; I believe that would have put dollars and dollars more into the pockets of the Canadian farmer to-day.
I am sorry I did not have an opportunity to prepare a speech like the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), who presented some valuable information to the house. He placed upon record many interesting figures, as he always does.

It is a pity if we emphasize all the unfortunate things and do not emphasize some of the better things that farmers have.
Here is something that I overlooked when speaking about New Zealand. I have in my hand a copy of a publication of the commercial intelligence bureau issued by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This is dated March 1 and gives a resume of the debts of various countries, including Canada, Australia and New Zealand, and the figures are on the same basis of exchange. The comparable figures show that in Canada we have a per capita debt of 62 pounds 5 shillings, while Australia's debt is 128 pounds per capita and New Zealand's comes to 182 pounds sterling.
I draw the attention of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) to the fact that if Nerv Zealand can produce butter as cheaply as he states, their prosperity should be such that they would not have got themselves involved in that amount of debt. It is very difficult for me to believe that if they can produce butter so cheaply in these countries they would be carrying such a load of debt. So, while we may have to stable our cattle, at least we have only one-third of the national obligation to carry that New Zealand has. I discovered the other day in a report furnished by the bureau of statistics that the New Zealander pays $5 per capita yearly for exchange alone on interest on the money he has borrowed on bonds redeemable in London. That is a fair indication that we have many things in Canada to be grateful for in spite of what we are told in the Globe and Mail.

It might be a good idea if we as farmers said, let us put an embargo on automobiles and go back to the horse and buggy, because we can grow hay and oats; that would stimulate the production of farm 
crops. That would be similar in my estimation to the arguments of some hon. members. I believe we would be just as much entitled to place a tax upon processed vegetable oils for revenue purposes, for no other reason than that I try to carry down here the same philosophy of life that I have applied in my own business. My experience in municipal affairs in the constituency I represent shows me the benefit of the policy of pay as you go. The Liberals have followed that policy practically since confederation. The Liberals are responsible for a very small part of our national debt to-day; much the larger part is a result of the expenditures of Conservative governments. My purpose in rising, Mr. Speaker, is to bring up to date some observations it was my privilege to make on this same question in 1936. As briefly as possible I should like to put a few facts on record. The most important is one which I believe we all realize, that in this day and age the animal kingdom is being considerably encroached upon by the vegetable kingdom. Canada is in a difficult position in that regard because naturally, on account of climate and occupation, Canada produces a large quantity of animal products.
The first observation I should like to make is that in the last few years the production of vegetable oils and vegetable oil products in Africa, the Straits Settlements, India, China and Manchuria has increased almost ten times. I shall not trouble the house with many figures, but in palm oil alone the increase has been from 268,000,000 pounds in 1920 to 1,000,000,000 pounds in 1937. In like manner importations into Canada have increased since the time this party was in power. When the Empire trade agreements were negotiated, our importations amounted to 90,000,000 pounds, and since then they have increased to 255,000,000 pounds. At the time the Empire trade agreements were negotiated in 1932, these importations did not constitute a very serious factor, because the world price level of these commodities was about ten cents a pound. However, on account of the tremendous increase in production-amounting to fourteen times in the case of palm oil in Sumatra-the price level has dropped from 10-9 cents a pound to less than four cents a pound. Hon. gentlemen opposite say we did nothing about it at that time; but, as the minister knows, we were careful to put section 18 in the empire trade agreements, which provides that any commodity covered by the agreements which interfered with the economy of any country within the empire might be dealt with.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-WITH RELATION TO DAIRYING, LIVE STOCK AND VEGETABLE OILS
speechtext:
And action. Canada's position becomes more pronounced year by year. Our friends in the United States, which is the largest consumer of fats and oils, little by little have applied taxes and tariffs of
all types and sorts against imports of oils and fats of all kinds, including fish oils, animal oils and vegetable oils. For example, first they imposed a revenue tax of two cents a pound; then, in addition, a processing tax of 4$ cents a pound in the case of cocoanut oil, which is a very large item. Then they imposed a tax of one cent a pound on palm kernel oil and a processing tax of three cents a pound. Just take palm oil alone. Back in 1932-33, when the empire agreements were negotiated, 287,594 pounds of palm oil came into Canada. In the year which closed on December 31, 1938, however, 70,360,100 pounds were imported. On the other hand, formerly only ten or fifteen per cent of the palm oil production could be used in food products, but now that figure has gone up to fifty-six per cent.
In the minute or two I have left I should like to answer a question asked by the hon. gentleman who said he was in favour of a revenue tax, and to show what has actually happened in the United States. In 1936 the United States imported 2,115,000,000 pounds of vegetable oils. When they put on their tax, it did not have the effect of stopping these importations. The vegetable oils came in just the same, except that there was a reduction of twenty per cent, as the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn) has said. Importations last year dropped to 1,647,446,000 pounds. In the meantime the revenue which has poured into the exchequer of the United States as a result of the imposition of these duties amounts to well over $80,000,000 annually since 1936. We are one-tenth or one-eleventh as large as the United States, so it would appear only reasonable to expect that as a result of putting our farmers on the same basis as the United States farmers we would automatically bring to the treasury of Canada at least $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 annually, at a very conservative estimate.

speechtext: If my hon. friend would permit me to ask a question, just for information, does the United States tax apply to the processing of all oils or only to the edible part? How do they deal with that?

speechtext:
It applies to all vegetable oils imported into that country. Of course some of these taxes are excise duties; some are processing taxes; but by and large, while some rates run as high as eight and nine cents a pound, the average would be about five cents.
Just before I resume my seat I should like to direct the minister's attention to what is happening at the present time in Washington.
2168	COMMONS
Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
This morning I received an Associated Press dispatch dated February 28, which stated that a movement was on foot, headed by the United States senator from Texas, to have the excise duty of three cents a pound, which was largely responsible for bringing $80,000,000 of revenue to the treasury of the United States, increased to five cents a pound.
The same thing is happening in Australia. Since this matter was last discussed I am informed that the government of Australia has been asked by the Queensland butter board to impose an excise duty sufficient to bring the cost of these butter substitutes up to the best price paid for the finest grade of creamery butter. Here we have two contrasting attitudes: These vegetable oils are brought to Canada in boat-loads-not rowboats but tank steamers-at less than four cents a pound, while in Australia the government is being requested to increase the duty to around nine cents. We want at least a revenue excise tax placed on vegetable oils similar to that which is imposed in the United States.
The only other point I should like to make before I resume my seat is that prior to the United States revenue bill of 1936, as amended by Senator Bailey, Canada enjoyed the full benefit of the largest fat-consuming market in the world, namely the United States. That was automatically cut off when the Bailey amendment went into effect.
